Q120306.t: Canada's highest summit, afloat on a sea of ice
Q120306.s: Nothing about Mount Logan is small. Its summit plateau runs for roughly 20 km, and the massif is thought to have the broadest base of any non-volcanic mountain on Earth. At 5,959 m it is the highest point in Canada, rising out of the glaciers of the St. Elias Mountains and still only about five kilometres short of cruise height.
Q120306.w: A huge, flat-topped white massif above a maze of glaciers, inland from the Gulf of Alaska near the Yukon–Alaska border.
f: It is named after William Logan, founder of the Geological Survey of Canada.
In North America only Denali, in Alaska, is higher.
Its glaciers lie in Kluane National Park, part of a UNESCO World Heritage site shared with Alaska.

q.q: Which is the only North American peak higher than Mount Logan?

Q870063.t: Where the Himalayas make their last snowy stand
Q870063.s: At the far eastern end of the Himalayas, just before the mountains bend south into the tropics, one pyramid still carries heavy snow. Hkakabo Razi, 5,881 m, is the highest mountain in Myanmar and in all of Southeast Asia. Its slopes fall from glaciers to dense subtropical forest, and the area is so remote that the first confirmed ascent came only in 1996.
Q870063.w: White peaks rising from dark, forested ridges in Myanmar's far north, close to the borders with India and China.
f: It is the highest mountain in Southeast Asia.
The first confirmed ascent, in 1996, was made by Japanese climber Takashi Ozaki and Tibetan climber Nyima Gyaltsen.
Meltwater from its glaciers feeds the headwaters of the Irrawaddy, Myanmar's great river.

q.q: When was Hkakabo Razi first climbed?

ne-pk-1159105475.t: The snowy crown over the Silk Road oases
ne-pk-1159105475.s: Silk Road caravans owed their water to ice like this. Kangze'gyai, 5,808 m, is the highest summit of the Qilian Mountains, the snowy wall on the north-eastern rim of the Tibetan Plateau. Its meltwater runs down to the Hexi Corridor, a chain of oases squeezed between these ridges and the Gobi, which the old trade route followed towards Central Asia.
ne-pk-1159105475.w: Snow-streaked ridges and small glaciers between the brown Tibetan uplands and a flat, desert-edged corridor to the north.
f: The Qilian Mountains run for roughly 800 km along the border of Qinghai and Gansu.
Qilian is thought to come from a Xiongnu word for 'sky'.
Jiayuguan, the western end of the Ming Great Wall, stands in the corridor at the foot of the Qilian range.

q.q: Which ancient trade route ran along the foot of the Qilian Mountains?

Q578862.t: Permanent snow 40 km from Caribbean beaches
Q578862.s: Palm-fringed beaches and permanent snow sit only about 40 km apart here. The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta climbs straight from the Caribbean to 5,775 m at Pico Cristóbal Colón, which makes it the highest coastal range on Earth. Its twin summit, Pico Simón Bolívar, is practically the same height, and the massif stands alone, cut off from the Andes by lowlands.
Q578862.w: An isolated, often cloud-capped mountain block rising from the Caribbean shore behind the city of Santa Marta, east of Barranquilla.
f: The massif spans almost every climate zone, from tropical coast to glacier.
The Kogi, Arhuaco and Wiwa peoples live on its slopes and call it the heart of the world.
Pico Cristóbal Colón is named after Christopher Columbus.

q.q: What record does the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta hold?

Q238147.t: Mexico's 'star mountain', seen from the Gulf coast
Q238147.s: On a clear day this white cone shows above the coastal haze near Veracruz, more than 100 km away. Pico de Orizaba, 5,636 m, is the highest mountain in Mexico and the third-highest in North America. Its Nahuatl name, Citlaltépetl, means 'star mountain'. The volcano has been quiet since the 19th century, and it carries the largest glaciers left in Mexico.
Q238147.w: A lone, symmetrical white cone east of Puebla, standing well above the volcanic highlands and the green slopes falling towards the Gulf.
f: Only Denali and Mount Logan are higher in North America.
The summit lies on the border of the states of Puebla and Veracruz.
Its Nahuatl name, Citlaltépetl, means 'star mountain'.

q.q: What does Citlaltépetl, the Nahuatl name of Pico de Orizaba, mean?

Q40758.t: Asia's tallest volcano, still breathing sulphur
Q40758.s: A white cone rises above the Alborz ridges, so neat it looks set down by hand. Damavand, 5,610 m, is Iran's highest mountain and the tallest volcano in Asia. Near the top, vents still breathe sulphur and warm gas. In the Persian epic Shahnameh, the tyrant Zahhak is chained inside this mountain, and the Caspian Sea lies just beyond the range.
Q40758.w: A lone snow-capped cone standing above the brown Alborz range, between Tehran and the green Caspian coast.
f: On clear days Damavand can be seen from Tehran, about 65 km away.
Yellow sulphur deposits and gas vents mark the summit area.
In the Shahnameh, the hero Fereydun imprisons the tyrant Zahhak inside Damavand.

q.q: In which mountain range does Damavand stand?

Q1037396.t: Glaciers above one of the lowest basins on Earth
Q1037396.s: The contrast here is extreme. Bogda Peak lifts its glaciers to 5,445 m, while the Turpan Depression, about 130 km to the south, sinks to around 150 m below sea level. Ürümqi spreads along the western foot of this eastern arm of the Tian Shan. Tucked into the northern slopes lies Tianchi, the 'Heavenly Lake', a narrow blue lake framed by spruce forest.
Q1037396.w: A three-headed snowy massif east of Ürümqi, with the pale Turpan basin to the south and the Dzungarian plain to the north.
f: Bogda means 'holy' in Mongolian.
Tianchi, the lake on its northern side, lies at about 1,900 m.
The Turpan Depression south of the range is one of the deepest dry basins on any continent.

q.q: What does the name Bogda mean in Mongolian?

ne-pk-1159106095.t: The smoking mountain beside the sleeping woman
ne-pk-1159106095.s: Look for the plume. Popocatépetl, 'smoking mountain' in Nahuatl, is one of Mexico's most active volcanoes, and a thread of steam or ash often drifts from its crater. Its neat cone, about 5,420 m high, stands beside the long ridge of Iztaccíhuatl, whose outline resembles a woman lying down. Mexico City lies about 70 km to the north-west.
ne-pk-1159106095.w: A symmetrical snowy cone, often trailing a plume, next to a long jagged white ridge south-east of Mexico City.
f: The pass between Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl is named after Hernán Cortés, whose army crossed it in 1519.
Sixteenth-century monasteries on its slopes are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Its current phase of activity began in 1994, after decades of quiet.

q.q: Which volcano forms a pair with Popocatépetl?

Q2648857.t: Andean glaciers at the edge of the endless plains
Q2648857.s: On the eastern side of Colombia's Andes, a short chain of glaciers hangs above the Llanos, the grassy plains that roll on towards Venezuela. Ritacuba Blanco, 5,410 m, is the highest of these peaks and the top of the whole Cordillera Oriental. Below the ice lie páramos, wet highlands dotted with frailejones, silver-leaved plants that stand in the mist like people.
Q2648857.w: A short line of white peaks on the eastern edge of the Andes, with flat green plains stretching away beyond them.
f: It is the highest point of the Sierra Nevada del Cocuy, in El Cocuy National Park.
The glaciers of El Cocuy have been shrinking fast in recent decades.
Frailejones, the rosette plants of the páramo, grow only about a centimetre a year.

q.q: Ritacuba Blanco is the highest point of which Andean range?

Q233351.t: An ice-capped volcano above Colombia's coffee hills
Q233351.s: Ice and fire share this summit. Nevado del Ruiz, 5,311 m, is an active volcano whose broad top is capped by glaciers, and a column of steam often rises from its crater, Arenas. Around it stretch the páramos of Los Nevados National Park. Lower down begin the steep green hills of the coffee region, a landscape listed by UNESCO.
Q233351.w: A broad, white-capped dome, sometimes steaming, rising above green ridges south-east of the city of Manizales.
f: Its summit crater is called Arenas.
Colombia's Coffee Cultural Landscape, on the hills below the volcano, joined the UNESCO list in 2011.
Its ice cap has shrunk sharply since the middle of the 20th century.

q.q: Which crop shapes the landscape on the hills below Nevado del Ruiz?

Q21519918.t: A white wall above the lake that never freezes
Q21519918.s: Behind the town of Karakol the Terskey Ala-Too rises like a white wall, and Pik Karakol, about 5,200 m, is one of its highest summits. To the north lies Issyk-Kul, a deep blue lake some 180 km long whose name means 'warm lake': even in the harsh Tian Shan winter it does not freeze. Snow and deep blue meet sharply here.
Q21519918.w: Snowy ridges on the south-eastern shore of Issyk-Kul, the long blue lake cradled in the Tian Shan.
f: Issyk-Kul lies at about 1,600 m and is up to roughly 670 m deep.
Its slightly salty water never freezes, even in winter.
The explorer Nikolai Przhevalsky died in Karakol in 1888, and the town long bore his name.

q.q: Which lake lies at the foot of Pik Karakol's range?

Q217457.t: The crown of a twelve-kilometre wall of ice
Q217457.s: Along the main Caucasus ridge runs the Bezengi Wall, some 12 km of ice and rock, and Shkhara, about 5,200 m, is its highest point. It is also the highest summit of Georgia. At its southern foot, the stone-towered villages of Upper Svaneti are among the highest permanently inhabited places in Europe, at around 2,100 m.
Q217457.w: A continuous white wall of summits on the main Caucasus ridge, south-east of Elbrus, with deep green valleys to the south.
f: The Bezengi Wall carries several peaks above 5,000 m.
Upper Svaneti, below Shkhara's southern face, has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1996.
The Enguri River rises from Shkhara's glaciers.

q.q: Shkhara is the highest summit of which country?

Q172070.t: Ice and jagged teeth right beside the equator
Q172070.s: The equator crosses its northern slopes, yet there is ice up here. Mount Kenya is the worn-down core of an ancient volcano, and its jagged central peaks, Batian at 5,199 m and Nelion close behind, are second in Africa only to Kilimanjaro. The country took its name from the mountain, which the Kikuyu call Kirinyaga and traditionally see as the seat of God.
Q172070.w: A broad, dark mountain with a rocky, snow-flecked crown, rising from farmland and forest north of Nairobi.
f: The equator runs across the mountain's northern slopes.
Its glaciers have lost most of their ice since the early 20th century.
Mount Kenya's national park and forest are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: Which is the highest peak of Mount Kenya?

Q72303.t: A lone giant with an ice cap and an ancient legend
Q72303.s: Few mountains stand so alone. Ararat rises more than four kilometres above the surrounding plains to 5,137 m, a dormant volcano capped with ice, with its smaller twin, Lesser Ararat, beside it like an echo. The Book of Genesis says Noah's ark came to rest 'upon the mountains of Ararat', and tradition has attached the story to this peak for centuries.
Q72303.w: A huge white-capped cone with a smaller, sharper cone beside it, standing alone above brown plains near the Aras River.
f: Lesser Ararat, nearly 3,900 m high, is joined to the main peak by a high saddle.
The summit carries a permanent ice cap.
Its Turkish name is Ağrı Dağı.

q.q: What is the Turkish name of Mount Ararat?

Q20191405.t: The high point of the Koh-e Baba, above Bamyan
Q20191405.s: In the heart of Afghanistan the land folds into the Koh-e Baba, a long, bare range often streaked with snow well into summer. Shāh Fōlādī, 5,048 m, is its highest summit. It towers over the Bamyan valley to the north, where green fields follow the river between red and ochre cliffs. Around the peak there are almost no trees: only stone, snow and sky.
Q20191405.w: A snowy, bare ridge running east–west in central Afghanistan, with the green thread of the Bamyan valley along its northern side.
f: The Koh-e Baba is a westward continuation of the Hindu Kush.
The Bamyan valley at its foot lies at about 2,500 m.
Band-e Amir, a chain of vivid blue lakes behind natural travertine dams, lies west of Bamyan.

q.q: Which valley lies at the northern foot of Shāh Fōlādī?

Q213704.s: Mérida fills a long terrace deep in the Venezuelan Andes, and the country's highest peak rises almost straight above it. Pico Bolívar, 4,980 m, is a sharp rock summit named after Simón Bolívar, with a bust of the Liberator on top. From the city, a cable car climbs to neighbouring Pico Espejo, and at over 4,700 m its top station is one of the highest in the world.
Q213704.w: A dark, sharp summit above a deep valley with a city on its terraced floor, in the north-eastern arm of the Andes.
f: It is the highest point of Venezuela.
A bust of Simón Bolívar stands on the summit.
The Mérida cable car, called Mukumbarí, reopened in 2016.

q.q: Which city lies at the foot of Pico Bolívar?

Q221666.t: Equatorial ice on the Mountains of the Moon
Q221666.s: Ice on the equator sounds impossible, yet the Rwenzori range carries glaciers, and Mount Stanley is its highest block. Its top, Margherita Peak, at about 5,000 m, is the third-highest point in Africa after Kilimanjaro and Mount Kenya. Cloud hides the massif on most days, and it has long been linked with Ptolemy's legendary 'Mountains of the Moon', the source of the Nile.
Q221666.w: A cloud-wrapped massif with white patches of ice, rising on the Uganda–Congo border west of Lake George.
f: The mountain is named after the explorer Henry Morton Stanley.
Its main summits were first climbed in 1906 by an expedition led by the Duke of the Abruzzi.
Margherita Peak is named after Queen Margherita of Italy.

q.q: Who is Margherita Peak, Mount Stanley's summit, named after?

Q1045888.t: The highest island summit on Earth, with tropical ice
Q1045888.s: In 1623 the Dutch navigator Jan Carstensz reported snow on a mountain near the equator, and people back home laughed. He was right. Puncak Jaya, 4,884 m, is the highest peak of New Guinea and of any island on Earth. Its grey limestone walls still hold small, fast-shrinking glaciers, surrounded by rainforest that runs down towards the sea.
Q1045888.w: Grey limestone cliffs with small white patches of ice, rising above a sea of green forest in the centre of New Guinea.
f: It was first climbed in 1962 by a team led by Heinrich Harrer.
It is often called the highest point between the Himalayas and the Andes.
It is also known as Carstensz Pyramid, after the navigator who reported its snow.

q.q: Who first reported snow on Puncak Jaya, in 1623?

Q210252.t: Eurasia's tallest active volcano, a near-perfect cone
Q210252.s: Eruptions here are almost routine. Klyuchevskaya Sopka, 4,750 m, is the highest active volcano in Eurasia, a steep, nearly perfect cone that often sends ash plumes drifting over Kamchatka. It rises from a crowded family of about a dozen volcanoes, and its snow is frequently streaked grey with fresh ash. From cruise height its crater is only about six kilometres below.
Q210252.w: A tall, symmetrical snow cone, often with a plume, in a cluster of volcanoes beside the broad Kamchatka River valley.
f: It is named after the village of Klyuchi at its foot.
It belongs to the 'Volcanoes of Kamchatka' UNESCO World Heritage site.
Its height changes by tens of metres as eruptions build up or blast away the summit.

q.q: On which peninsula does Klyuchevskaya Sopka stand?

Q13171265.t: A summit named after the hero of a vast epic
Q13171265.s: The Kyrgyz epic Manas is among the longest poems ever recorded, and this summit carries its hero's name. At 4,482 m, Manas Peak crowns the Talas Ala-Too, a rugged western arm of the Tian Shan with small glaciers and deep gorges. North of the ridge the mountains drop towards the Kazakh plains, where the Aksu-Zhabagly reserve has guarded the slopes since 1926.
Q13171265.w: A snowy knot of summits at the western end of the Tian Shan, where green valleys open north onto the plains of southern Kazakhstan.
f: Some versions of the Manas epic run to hundreds of thousands of lines.
Aksu-Zhabagly, founded in 1926, is the oldest nature reserve in Central Asia.
Near the town of Talas, east of the peak, a 14th-century mausoleum is traditionally called the tomb of Manas.

q.q: Who is Manas in Kyrgyz culture?
q.a: The hero of a national epic

Q20190966.t: A lonely 4,000-metre summit in Afghanistan's highlands
Q20190966.s: Deep in the south-west of Afghanistan's central highlands, the ridges still climb above 4,000 m before breaking up towards the deserts. Kuh-e Jang Qal'eh reaches 4,171 m, a bare summit that keeps its snow through winter and into spring. From cruise height it is less than seven kilometres away, amid folded brown ridges cut by dry valleys.
Q20190966.w: Bare, brown folded ridges with snow on the highest crests, where Afghanistan's central mountains fade south-west into lower, drier country.
f: In Persian, kuh means 'mountain' and qal'eh means 'fortress'.
Snowmelt from these highlands feeds rivers that run south-west towards the Sistan basin on the Iranian border.

q.q: What does the Persian word kuh, which starts many peak names, mean?

Q60967.t: Borneo's granite crown above the morning cloud
Q60967.s: Kinabalu's top is a jagged plateau of bare granite, grey spires poking through the morning cloud above Borneo's green hills. At about 4,100 m it is the highest mountain on the island. Its slopes pass from lowland rainforest through mossy cloud forest to naked rock, and they hold one of the richest collections of plants on Earth, giant pitcher plants included.
Q60967.w: A grey, jagged granite massif rising abruptly from green hills near Borneo's north-west coast, east of Kota Kinabalu.
f: Kinabalu Park became Malaysia's first UNESCO World Heritage site in 2000.
Its highest point, Low's Peak, is named after Hugh Low, a British official who explored the summit plateau in 1851.
For the Kadazan-Dusun people, the mountain is a resting place for the spirits of the dead.

q.q: Who is Low's Peak, the summit of Kinabalu, named after?

ne-pk-1159105699.t: Snow on the border above Baikal's little sister
ne-pk-1159105699.s: Where Siberia meets Mongolia, the Eastern Sayan ends in a snowy peak with small glaciers clinging to its flanks. Mönkh Saridag, 3,491 m, is the highest point of the range, and the Russia–Mongolia border runs across its summit. Just to the south stretches Khövsgöl, a long, clear mountain lake whose water eventually flows north into Lake Baikal.
ne-pk-1159105699.w: A white-topped massif just north of the long blue Lake Khövsgöl, at the southern edge of the Siberian taiga.
f: It is the highest peak of the Eastern Sayan mountains.
Lake Khövsgöl holds roughly 70% of Mongolia's fresh water.
Khövsgöl drains through the Selenga River system into Lake Baikal.

q.q: Into which lake does water from nearby Khövsgöl eventually flow?

Q120314.t: Five flat summits of a sacred Buddhist mountain
Q120314.s: Five broad, almost flat-topped summits give this mountain its name: Wutai means 'five terraces'. At 3,058 m, its northern terrace is often called the roof of northern China. For well over a thousand years it has been one of the four sacred mountains of Chinese Buddhism, and dozens of temples fill the valleys between the terraces, far too small to pick out from the air.
Q120314.w: A cluster of broad, grassy, rounded summits above the loess hills of north-eastern Shanxi, west of the long Taihang ridges.
f: Mount Wutai joined the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2009.
The main hall of Nanchan Temple here, dated to 782, is one of the oldest surviving timber buildings in China.
Tradition links the mountain to Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom.

q.q: What does the name Wutai mean?

Q1061148.t: The high point of Córdoba's rolling sierras
Q1061148.s: Rising from the flat Pampas, the Sierras de Córdoba look like long waves of grey granite and golden grass. Their highest point is Cerro Champaquí, nearly 2,800 m, a broad rounded summit rather than a sharp peak. To the east lies the Calamuchita valley with its blue reservoirs; to the west, the drier Traslasierra valley. Some winters bring snow to the top.
Q1061148.w: A broad grassy dome on a north–south line of low sierras, with blue reservoirs in the valley to the east and flat pampas beyond.
f: It is the highest point of Argentina's Córdoba province.
The Sierras de Córdoba belong to the Sierras Pampeanas, ancient blocks of crystalline rock tilted up above the plains.

q.q: Champaquí is the highest point of which Argentine province?

Q3321738.t: An Arctic giant demoted by better measurements
Q3321738.s: For decades this was thought to be the tallest peak of the Brooks Range. Then, in 2014, precise new surveys showed two neighbours to be slightly higher, and Mount Chamberlin, about 2,700 m, slipped to third place. It rises in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, well north of the Arctic Circle, where snowy ridges fall away to the tundra of the coastal plain.
Q3321738.w: Snow-streaked, glaciated peaks on the northern edge of the Brooks Range, with flat tundra stretching north to the Beaufort Sea.
f: It is named after Thomas Chrowder Chamberlin, an American geologist.
Mount Isto, about 50 km to the east-south-east, is now counted as the highest peak of the Brooks Range.
The Arctic National Wildlife Refuge covers nearly 80,000 km².

q.q: Which peak is now counted as the highest in the Brooks Range?

ne-gl-albanov-ice-cap.t: A white dome on one of the last-mapped archipelagos
ne-gl-albanov-ice-cap.s: Severnaya Zemlya was one of the last sizeable archipelagos to reach the map: it was discovered only in 1913. On October Revolution Island, its largest island, several ice domes merge into one frozen landscape, and the Albanov Ice Cap is one of them. It shows as a smooth, pale dome whose edges break up where the ice meets grey rock or the sea.
ne-gl-albanov-ice-cap.w: A smooth white dome among neighbouring ice caps on October Revolution Island, with the Kara Sea to the west.
f: It is named after Valerian Albanov, navigator of the Arctic ship Svyataya Anna.
Georgy Ushakov and Nikolai Urvantsev first mapped Severnaya Zemlya in detail in 1930–32.
Close to half of Severnaya Zemlya is covered by glaciers.

q.q: In which archipelago is the Albanov Ice Cap?

ne-gl-barentsjokulen.t: An ice cap named after the man who found Svalbard
ne-gl-barentsjokulen.s: In 1596 the Dutch navigator Willem Barentsz sighted a land of jagged peaks and named it Spitsbergen. This ice cap, Barentsjøkulen, bears his name. It covers the heart of Barentsøya, a quiet island in eastern Svalbard, and spreads as a pale dome between dark, flat-topped mountains. Its only neighbours are reindeer, walruses and polar bears.
ne-gl-barentsjokulen.w: A smooth white dome filling the centre of an island east of Spitsbergen, ringed by dark cliffs and, often, sea ice.
f: Barentsøya, the island it covers, has no permanent inhabitants.
Barentsz reached Spitsbergen in 1596 while searching for a north-east passage to Asia.
The Barents Sea, to the south, is also named after him.

q.q: Which navigator gave his name to Barentsjøkulen?

ne-gl-eyjafjallajokull.t: The glacier volcano that grounded Europe's planes
ne-gl-eyjafjallajokull.s: Every air traveller has a reason to remember this name. In April 2010 the volcano beneath Eyjafjallajökull erupted through its ice, and its fine ash drifted over Europe, closing much of the continent's airspace for days. From above it looks modest: a rounded white cap on a mountain near Iceland's south coast. The name simply means 'glacier of the island mountains'.
ne-gl-eyjafjallajokull.w: A small, rounded ice cap above green coastal lowlands in southern Iceland, just west of the larger Mýrdalsjökull.
f: About 100,000 flights were cancelled during the 2010 ash crisis.
The mountain under the ice reaches about 1,650 m.
The 2010 eruption began on the Fimmvörðuháls pass beside the glacier, then moved to the summit crater under the ice.

q.q: What does the name Eyjafjallajökull mean?

ne-gl-hang-ten-icefield.t: Wild ice in a corner of Canada with no roads
ne-gl-hang-ten-icefield.s: The Coast Mountains of northern British Columbia hide icefields that few people ever hear of, and the Hang Ten Icefield is one of them. About 10 km across, it lies just inland of the vast Juneau Icefield and the Alaska border. It shows as a patch of white among steep, dark peaks, with glaciers spilling into valleys that no road reaches.
ne-gl-hang-ten-icefield.w: A compact white icefield among steep dark peaks, east of the huge Juneau Icefield and south of long Atlin Lake.
f: It lies in the Boundary Ranges, the northern part of the Coast Mountains.
There are no permanent settlements anywhere near the icefield.
Devils Paw, on the Alaska border to the south-west, is the highest summit of the Juneau Icefield.

q.q: Which huge icefield lies just west of the Hang Ten Icefield?

ne-gl-hofsjokull.t: A dome of ice hiding a volcano in Iceland's empty heart
ne-gl-hofsjokull.s: In the middle of Iceland, between two famous highland tracks, sits an almost perfectly round dome of ice. Hofsjökull is the country's third-largest glacier, and beneath it lies an active volcano with a caldera. Its meltwater helps feed the Þjórsá, Iceland's longest river, which winds south across black sand and lava to the Atlantic.
ne-gl-hofsjokull.w: A round white dome in the grey-black desert of the central highlands, between Langjökull to the west and Vatnajökull to the east.
f: Hofsjökull covers roughly 900 km².
The Þjórsá, fed partly by its meltwater, is about 230 km long.
The Kjölur and Sprengisandur highland roads pass on either side of it.

q.q: Which is Iceland's longest river, fed partly by Hofsjökull?

ne-gl-hooker-icefield.t: Ice around the phantom giants of the Rockies
ne-gl-hooker-icefield.s: In 1827 the botanist David Douglas crossed Athabasca Pass and declared two nearby peaks, Mount Hooker and Mount Brown, the highest in North America, at over 16,000 feet. The legend lasted for decades until surveyors found them closer to 3,300 m. The Hooker Icefield spreads around Mount Hooker, a white plateau among the sharp ridges of the Canadian Rockies.
ne-gl-hooker-icefield.w: A white icefield on the crest of the Rockies south of Jasper, near the Alberta–British Columbia border.
f: Mount Hooker is named after botanist William Jackson Hooker, later director of Kew Gardens.
Athabasca Pass, nearby, was a main fur-trade route across the Rockies in the early 19th century.
David Douglas also gave his name to the Douglas fir.

q.q: Who started the legend of giant peaks near the Hooker Icefield?

ne-gl-jostedalsbreen.t: The largest glacier on mainland Europe
ne-gl-jostedalsbreen.s: Between the Sognefjord and the Nordfjord, a long white plateau of ice runs for some 60 km. Jostedalsbreen is the largest glacier in continental Europe, covering nearly 475 km², and dozens of blue-white tongues spill from it into green valleys. Some, like Briksdalsbreen and Nigardsbreen, end in milky meltwater lakes only a few hundred metres above sea level.
ne-gl-jostedalsbreen.w: A long white ice plateau with blue tongues reaching into valleys, between two of Norway's longest fjords.
f: The ice is up to about 600 m thick in places.
Jostedalsbreen National Park was established in 1991.
Around 50 outlet glaciers flow from the main ice plateau.

q.q: Between which two fjords does Jostedalsbreen lie?

ne-gl-langjokull.s: Its name means simply 'long glacier', and that is exactly how it looks: a pale, stretched-out ice cap running some 50 km across Iceland's western highlands. Langjökull is the country's second-largest glacier. At its eastern edge a tongue of ice reaches the lake Hvítárvatn, source of the Hvítá river, which later plunges over the famous Gullfoss waterfall.
ne-gl-langjokull.w: An elongated white ice cap running south-west to north-east, with a milky lake at its eastern edge and green farmland to the south.
f: Visitors can walk inside it through a man-made ice tunnel opened in 2015.
Geysir and Gullfoss, two of Iceland's best-known sights, lie within about 40 km of its southern edge.

q.q: What does the name Langjökull mean?

ne-gl-plateau-icefield.t: A high sheet of ice in the ranges beyond Whistler
ne-gl-plateau-icefield.s: A short flight north of Vancouver, the Coast Mountains turn into a wilderness of rock and ice. The Plateau Icefield, about 14 km across, is one of the many ice sheets of the Pacific Ranges, lying some 80 km north-west of Whistler, just south of the larger Lillooet Icecap. It shows as a smooth white table edged by dark, crevassed glacier tongues.
ne-gl-plateau-icefield.w: A flat white ice sheet among steep dark peaks, north-west of Whistler and just south of a larger, rounder icecap.
f: The icefields of the Pacific Ranges are among the largest in the world's temperate latitudes.
The icefield lies about 150 km north-north-west of Vancouver.

q.q: In which mountain system is the Plateau Icefield?

ne-gl-rusanov-ice-cap.t: An Arctic ice dome between the Kara and Laptev seas
ne-gl-rusanov-ice-cap.s: Severnaya Zemlya is a barrier of islands and ice between the Kara Sea and the Laptev Sea, and the Rusanov Ice Cap sits on its largest island, October Revolution. Some 20 km across, it forms a smooth, gently rounded dome. Sea ice surrounds it for most of the year, and in the brief summer its edges turn grey where meltwater and rock show through.
ne-gl-rusanov-ice-cap.w: A broad, rounded white dome on the northern side of October Revolution Island, one of several ice caps lying side by side.
f: It is named after Vladimir Rusanov, a geologist who explored Novaya Zemlya in the early 1900s.
The islands of Severnaya Zemlya separate the Kara Sea from the Laptev Sea.
The archipelago lies just over 1,000 km from the North Pole.

q.q: Which two seas does Severnaya Zemlya separate?
x: The Laptev and East Siberian seas

ne-gl-svartisen.t: The 'black ice' that reaches down towards a fjord
ne-gl-svartisen.s: Just north of the Arctic Circle, Norway's second-largest glacier spreads over the mountains in two great sheets. Svartisen means 'the black ice', perhaps for the dark blue sheen of its tongues. One of them, Engabreen, flows down almost to the waters of Holandsfjorden, making it one of the lowest-reaching glaciers on mainland Europe.
ne-gl-svartisen.w: Two large white ice sheets on the mountains near Norway's coast, with tongues reaching towards a fjord, just north of the Arctic Circle.
f: Svartisen covers roughly 370 km² in two main parts, Vestisen and Østisen.
Scientists study the underside of Engabreen from tunnels built for a hydropower scheme beneath the ice.
The Arctic Circle crosses Saltfjellet–Svartisen National Park.

q.q: What does the Norwegian name Svartisen mean?

ne-gl-sydkap-ice-cap.t: Ice on the south shore of Canada's northernmost island
ne-gl-sydkap-ice-cap.s: Ellesmere Island reaches closer to the North Pole than any other part of Canada, and its southern coast is crowned by the Sydkap Ice Cap, some 40 km across. The Norwegian name means 'south cape', given by Otto Sverdrup's expedition around 1900. Glaciers spill from the dome towards Jones Sound, a channel locked in ice for much of the year.
ne-gl-sydkap-ice-cap.w: A broad white ice cap on Ellesmere's southern coast, with glaciers running down to the frozen channel that separates it from Devon Island.
f: Otto Sverdrup's expedition aboard the Fram explored much of this coast in 1898–1902.
Grise Fiord, one of Canada's northernmost communities, lies roughly 90 km to the east.
Jones Sound, south of the ice cap, separates Ellesmere Island from Devon Island.

q.q: What does the Norwegian name Sydkap mean?

ne-gl-vavilov-ice-cap.t: A sleepy Arctic ice cap that suddenly began to race
ne-gl-vavilov-ice-cap.s: For decades the Vavilov Ice Cap moved slowly, as cold polar ice caps do. Then, around 2013, its western edge suddenly sped up and began pushing out across the floor of the Kara Sea, advancing kilometres within a few years. Glaciologists watched in surprise: such a fast surge is rare in the dry, frozen High Arctic. It covers the western part of October Revolution Island.
ne-gl-vavilov-ice-cap.w: A white dome on the western side of October Revolution Island, with a broad lobe of ice pushed out into the sea.
f: Its western outlet began a dramatic surge around 2013, reaching speeds of many metres a day.
It lies on October Revolution Island, the largest island of Severnaya Zemlya.

q.q: What happened to the Vavilov Ice Cap around 2013?
q.a: Its edge surged out into the sea

Q587808.t: The ridge of white waters that built Johannesburg
Q587808.s: Gold turned this low ridge into a metropolis. The Witwatersrand, 'ridge of white waters' in Afrikaans, rises only a couple of hundred metres above the Highveld, yet after gold was found here in 1886, Johannesburg grew along it at astonishing speed. The rocks beneath have yielded a huge share of all the gold ever mined, and pale mine dumps still dot the city.
Q587808.w: A low east–west ridge on high grassland, with Johannesburg's sprawl and pale yellow mine dumps strung along it.
f: Rocks of the Witwatersrand basin have produced roughly 40% of all the gold ever mined.
Rain north of the ridge drains to the Indian Ocean via the Limpopo; rain to the south, to the Atlantic via the Vaal and Orange.
Johannesburg was founded in 1886, the year of the gold discovery.

q.q: When was gold discovered on the Witwatersrand?

Q27496722.t: Dark heights between a sand sea and the Tibesti
Q27496722.s: Deep in the Libyan Sahara, south of the dunes of the Murzuq sand sea, the ground rises into the dark, rocky heights of Jabal Bin Ghunaymah. They reach only about 1,000 m, but in this flat emptiness they stand out clearly: brown and black rock cut by dry wadis, with pale sand drifting into every hollow. Beneath some wadi beds, water lies close to the surface.
Q27496722.w: Dark, rocky uplands cut by pale dry valleys, between the orange dunes of the Murzuq sand sea and the Tibesti massif to the south-east.
f: The heights reach roughly 1,000 m above sea level.
Rainfall here averages only a few tens of millimetres a year.

q.q: Which sand sea lies north of Jabal Bin Ghunaymah?

Q1501766.t: A long volcanic ridge where counting may have begun
Q1501766.s: For some 800 km a narrow line of hills runs north–south between the high bushveld and the coastal plain of Mozambique. The Lebombo Mountains are made of old volcanic rock and are mostly only a few hundred metres high, yet they form a clear wall. In Border Cave, in the southern Lebombos, archaeologists found a notched baboon bone about 43,000 years old, one of the oldest known counting tools.
Q1501766.w: A thin, straight line of low hills running north–south, with Maputo and the flat coastal plain to the east and bushveld to the west.
f: The Lebombo bone is a baboon fibula carrying 29 notches.
The ridge marks much of the eastern edge of Kruger National Park.
Parts of the borders of South Africa, Eswatini and Mozambique follow its crest.

q.q: What ancient object was found in the Lebombo Mountains?

Q1433137.t: Cedar forests and snow in the heart of Morocco
Q1433137.s: Between Fès and the High Atlas, Morocco turns unexpectedly green and cool. The Middle Atlas is a land of limestone plateaus, extinct volcanic cones and dark forests of Atlas cedar, where Barbary macaques live. Snow falls here most winters, and the town of Ifrane, with its steep red roofs, is nicknamed the Switzerland of Morocco.
Q1433137.w: Dark patches of cedar forest on limestone plateaus and rounded volcanic cones, between the plain of Fès and the higher, drier Atlas to the south.
f: Ifrane recorded −23.9 °C in 1935, often cited as the lowest temperature ever measured in Africa.
The Oum Er-Rbia, one of Morocco's longest rivers, rises in the Middle Atlas.
The Barbary macaque is the only wild primate north of the Sahara apart from humans.

q.q: Which monkey lives in the cedar forests of the Middle Atlas?

Q1868712.t: Sierra Leone's rooftop above the rainforest
Q1868712.s: In north-eastern Sierra Leone the forest suddenly climbs onto a granite massif. The Loma Mountains carry the country's highest peak, Bintumani, about 1,945 m, whose rounded top is covered not in trees but in grassland. Montane forest on the slopes shelters chimpanzees, and not far to the north-east, in the highlands of Guinea, the great Niger River begins its journey.
Q1868712.w: A dark green massif with grassy, rounded tops rising from the forest and farmland of north-eastern Sierra Leone.
f: Bintumani, also called Loma Mansa, is the highest point of Sierra Leone.
The source of the Niger lies in the Guinea Highlands, just across the border to the north-east.

q.q: What is the highest peak of Sierra Leone?

Q533041.t: Blinding salt flats where a great lake once lay
Q533041.s: The Makgadikgadi looks like a vast white stain on the Kalahari, blinding under the midday sun. These salt pans are the dried-out floor of a huge ancient lake, and together they rank among the largest salt flats on Earth. After good rains a thin sheet of water returns, and tens of thousands of flamingos arrive to feed and breed.
Q533041.w: Brilliant white flats edged by grey-green scrub in north-eastern Botswana, with two main pans lying side by side.
f: The two largest pans are called Sowa and Ntwetwe.
Kubu Island, a granite outcrop crowned with old baobabs, rises from the salt like a ship.
Large herds of zebra migrate to the grasslands around the pans in the rainy season.

q.q: What did the Makgadikgadi Pans once hold?

Q1067917.t: A black stain of lava in the middle of the Sahara
Q1067917.s: A dark blot seems to have spilled across the pale centre of Libya. It is Haruj, a vast volcanic field of black basalt, some 40,000 km² of lava flows dotted with more than a hundred cones and craters. Its full Arabic name, al-Haruj al-Aswad, means 'the black Haruj', and against the surrounding desert its outline is unmistakable even from orbit.
Q1067917.w: A huge dark patch of lava fields and small cones in central Libya, sharply outlined against the pale desert around it.
f: Al-Haruj al-Aswad means 'the black Haruj' in Arabic.
It is the largest volcanic field in Libya.

q.q: Which colour gives al-Haruj al-Aswad its name?

Q1740661.t: Folded hills where Namibia's plateau drops to the Namib
Q1740661.s: Some of Namibia's dizziest roads drop off the edge of this highland. West of Windhoek, the Khomas Highland, around 2,000 m high, crumples into endless ridges of grey-brown rock and golden grass, then breaks off abruptly in a great escarpment above the Namib Desert. Passes such as Spreetshoogte zigzag down it, from dry grassland to pale gravel plains and, further west, the dunes.
Q1740661.w: Tightly folded brown ridges west of Windhoek, ending in a steep escarpment above the flat, pale Namib plains.
f: The H.E.S.S. gamma-ray telescopes stand in the Khomas Highland, which is known for dark, clear skies.
Windhoek, Namibia's capital, lies at about 1,650 m on the eastern side of the highland.

q.q: Which capital city lies on the edge of the Khomas Highland?

Q1343339.t: Sandstone arches and desert crocodiles in the Sahara
Q1343339.s: Wind and ancient water have carved the Ennedi into a maze of sandstone towers, canyons and natural arches rising from the Sahara in north-eastern Chad. One arch, Aloba, stands roughly 120 m tall, among the highest in the world. In a shady gorge, the Guelta d'Archei, camels drink from a permanent pool where a few crocodiles still survive, relics of a greener Sahara.
Q1343339.w: A dark, deeply dissected block of sandstone with pale sand filling its canyons, rising from the flat desert of north-eastern Chad.
f: The Ennedi Massif became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2016.
Thousands of rock paintings show cattle, giraffes and people from the time of the green Sahara.
Its crocodiles are among the last left anywhere in the Sahara.

q.q: Which animals survive in the Guelta d'Archei pool?

Q811142.t: A cool granite island above Nigeria's plains
Q811142.s: Rising abruptly from the savanna, the Jos Plateau is a granite tableland around 1,200 m high, noticeably cooler than the country around it. Scattered across it are dozens of small lakes, many of them flooded pits left by more than a century of tin mining. Rivers flow off the plateau in every direction, feeding both the Niger and Lake Chad.
Q811142.w: A raised plateau of granite knobs and scattered small lakes, rising sharply from the surrounding savanna in central Nigeria.
f: The Nok culture, famous for terracotta heads over 2,000 years old, is named after a village near the plateau.
Large-scale tin mining began here in the early 20th century.
The city of Jos lies at about 1,200 m.

q.q: Which ancient culture, known for terracotta heads, is linked to this area?

Q1878522.t: Thousands of lakes glittering in the Siberian tundra
Q1878522.s: Between the long Gulf of Ob and the Taz Bay, the land seems to dissolve into water. The Taz Peninsula is flat tundra on permafrost, pocked with thousands of lakes that glitter like scattered glass when the sun is low. In winter it all turns into a single white sheet. Beneath it lies Yamburg, one of the giant gas fields of northern Siberia.
Q1878522.w: Flat, lake-speckled tundra between two wide Arctic bays: the Gulf of Ob to the west and the Taz Bay to the east.
f: Most of the peninsula lies north of the Arctic Circle.
The Yamburg gas field, one of the largest in the world, lies on the peninsula.

q.q: Which gulf lies west of the Taz Peninsula?

Q1470027.t: Where the Great Plains run into a wall of mountains
Q1470027.s: Flying west across the Great Plains, the first mountains you meet rise like a wall: the Front Range of the Rockies. Denver, Boulder and Colorado Springs line its foot, and several summits top 4,000 m. Pikes Peak, 4,302 m, stands out at the southern end; the view from its top in 1893 inspired the song 'America the Beautiful'.
Q1470027.w: The first high, often snow-streaked ridges west of the flat plains, with Denver and Colorado Springs spread along their foot.
f: Katharine Lee Bates wrote 'America the Beautiful' after reaching the top of Pikes Peak in 1893.
The highest summit of the Front Range is Grays Peak, about 4,350 m.
Pikes Peak is named after Zebulon Pike, who explored the region in 1806.

q.q: Which song was inspired by the view from Pikes Peak?

Q879014.t: The ridges that nearly stopped Lewis and Clark
Q879014.s: In September 1805, Lewis and Clark's expedition struggled over these mountains on snowy trails, short of food. The Bitterroot Range still looks forbidding: long, forested ridges and deep valleys stretching along the Idaho–Montana border, crossed by very few roads. In late spring the valleys bloom with pink bitterroot flowers, the plant that gave the range its name.
Q879014.w: Long, dark-green forested ridges running along the Idaho–Montana border, with few clearings and almost no roads.
f: The bitterroot, Montana's state flower, is called Lewisia rediviva after Meriwether Lewis.
The expedition crossed on the Lolo Trail, an old Nez Perce route.
The Selway-Bitterroot Wilderness here is one of the largest wilderness areas in the lower 48 states.

q.q: Which expedition crossed the Bitterroot Range in 1805?

Q1585051.t: Europe's largest high plateau, land of wild reindeer
Q1585051.s: Europe's biggest herd of wild reindeer roams this plateau. Hardangervidda, west of Oslo, is the largest mountain plateau in Europe: a vast, treeless tableland of lakes and bare rock, mostly between 1,100 and 1,400 m high. In winter it becomes one white plain; in summer, a patchwork of grey stone, green moss and countless blue lakes.
Q1585051.w: A broad, treeless plateau speckled with lakes, with the Hardangerjøkulen ice cap on its northern edge.
f: Hardangervidda National Park is the largest national park on the Norwegian mainland.
The Bergen Railway crosses its northern edge, reaching about 1,220 m at Finse.

q.q: Which wild animals form Europe's largest herd on Hardangervidda?

Q1464606.t: A dark island of mountains in Namibia's dry south
Q1464606.s: Southern Namibia is mostly flat, stony semi-desert, which makes the Great Karas Mountains stand out like an island. Their dark, flat-topped ridges rise well above the plains, deeply cut by gorges that carry water only after rare storms. The Fish River Canyon, one of the largest canyons in Africa, lies about 130 km to the west.
Q1464606.w: A dark, deeply cut block of flat-topped mountains standing above pale plains, south-east of the town of Keetmanshoop.
f: Keetmanshoop, to the north-west, is known for its nearby forest of quiver trees.
Namibia's southernmost region, ǁKaras, takes its name from these mountains.

q.q: Which famous canyon lies west of the Karas Mountains?

Q886772.t: A volcanic massif with crater lakes in Sudan's west
Q886772.s: Two small lakes lie inside a volcanic crater some 5 km wide at the top of Jebel Marra, the highest point of Sudan at about 3,000 m. This mountain island of volcanic rock rises from the dry savanna of western Sudan and catches rain the plains never get, so streams, orchards and green terraces cling to its slopes.
Q886772.w: A large, dark volcanic massif with a round summit caldera, rising far above the dry brown plains of western Sudan.
f: Jebel Marra is the highest point of Sudan.
Citrus and other fruit trees grow on its terraced slopes.

q.q: What lies in the summit caldera of Jebel Marra?

Q275491.t: Morocco's green arc facing the Mediterranean
Q275491.s: The Rif curves along Morocco's Mediterranean coast like a drawn bow, green on its seaward slopes and browner inland. Geologically it is only half of an arc: the same mountain belt swings across the Strait of Gibraltar and continues in southern Spain as the Betic Cordillera. On the highest ridges, above 2,000 m, grow forests of cedar and the rare Moroccan fir.
Q275491.w: A curved belt of steep green-and-brown ridges along Morocco's Mediterranean shore, between Tangier and the Algerian border.
f: The highest summit, Jbel Tidirhine, reaches about 2,450 m.
The blue-washed town of Chefchaouen lies in the western Rif.
With Spain's Betic Cordillera, the Rif forms the Gibraltar Arc.

q.q: Which Spanish mountains continue the Rif across the Strait of Gibraltar?

Q152294.t: Zimbabwe's misty rooftop in the Eastern Highlands
Q152294.s: Along Zimbabwe's eastern border the land rises into cool green uplands of grassland, pine plantations and tea estates. Their summit is Mount Nyangani, 2,592 m, the highest point in the country: a broad, heath-covered hilltop often wrapped in mist. To the south, the Mtarazi Falls drop over the escarpment in one of the highest waterfalls in Africa.
Q152294.w: Green rolling uplands with dark pine plantations, rising to a broad summit on Zimbabwe's border with Mozambique.
f: Mount Nyangani is the highest point of Zimbabwe.
Tea grows in the Honde Valley below the escarpment.

q.q: Mount Nyangani is the highest point of which country?

Q745846.t: Rocks that gave their name to a geological period
Q745846.s: A giant oval rim of rock rises out of the red land at the heart of the Flinders Ranges: Wilpena Pound, a natural amphitheatre about 17 km long. These folded ridges run for more than 400 km north from the Spencer Gulf. In nearby hills scientists found fossils of some of the earliest complex animals, and in 2004 a whole geological period, the Ediacaran, was named after them.
Q745846.w: Parallel red and grey ridges running north from the head of Spencer Gulf, with the oval rim of Wilpena Pound in the middle.
f: The Ediacaran, named after the Ediacara Hills, was the first new geological period added in over a century.
Wilpena Pound is a bowl-shaped fold of rock layers, not a volcanic crater.
The Adnyamathanha people call Wilpena Pound Ikara.

q.q: Which geological period is named after hills in the Flinders Ranges?

Q1475441.t: Red ribs of rock around Alice Springs
Q1475441.s: Right in the middle of Australia, long red ridges run east and west of Alice Springs like the ribs of a buried giant. The MacDonnell Ranges stretch for about 640 km, sliced by deep gaps and gorges where rivers cut straight through them. Among them rises the Finke, often called one of the oldest rivers in the world, which flows only after rain.
Q1475441.w: Long, parallel red ridges running east–west through the centre of Australia, with the small grid of Alice Springs in a gap.
f: Mount Zeil, about 1,530 m, is the highest point in the Northern Territory.
Explorer John McDouall Stuart named the ranges in 1860 after Governor Richard MacDonnell.
The Arrernte people are the traditional owners of the Alice Springs area.

q.q: Which town lies in a gap of the MacDonnell Ranges?

Q21961599.t: The wooded scarp that walls in Perth
Q21961599.s: A single long fault separates some of the oldest rocks on Earth from the young sands beneath Perth. Along it, east of the city, rises a dark-green wall, the Darling Scarp, edge of the Darling Range, with the ancient granite of the Yilgarn Craton behind it. On top grow jarrah forests, broken by reservoirs that supply Perth with water and by the red scars of bauxite mines.
Q21961599.w: A low, forested scarp running north–south just east of Perth, with the city and coastal plain to the west and reservoirs on top.
f: Its highest point, Mount Cooke, is only about 580 m high.
Jarrah, a eucalyptus with deep red wood, grows naturally only in south-western Australia.
The Yilgarn Craton behind the scarp holds rocks well over 2.5 billion years old.

q.q: Which city lies at the foot of the Darling Range?

Q649051.t: A volcanic spine along Sumatra's western shore
Q649051.s: Sumatra has a backbone, and it runs close to the island's western coast for some 1,700 km. The Barisan Mountains are a chain of forested ridges and smoking volcanoes, with the Indian Ocean on one side and wide lowland plains on the other. Their highest point, Mount Kerinci, about 3,800 m, is the tallest volcano in Indonesia, and tigers still roam the forests around it.
Q649051.w: Steep forested ridges and volcanic cones hugging Sumatra's west coast, with the Indian Ocean close by on one side.
f: Barisan means 'row' or 'line' in Indonesian.
Three national parks in the range form the UNESCO site Tropical Rainforest Heritage of Sumatra.
The Great Sumatran Fault runs along the length of the range.

q.q: What does the Indonesian word barisan mean?

Q733842.t: Siberian glaciers on the divide of two oceans
Q733842.s: Between the frozen uplands around Oymyakon and the Sea of Okhotsk rises one of the harshest ranges in Siberia. The Suntar-Khayata reaches nearly 3,000 m at Mus-Khaya and carries some two hundred small glaciers. It forms part of the divide between rivers draining to the Arctic Ocean and those running to the Sea of Okhotsk. Its grey, snow-streaked summits show no roads at all.
Q733842.w: Grey, snow-streaked jagged peaks with small glaciers, between the Yakutian uplands and the Okhotsk coast.
f: Its highest peak, Mus-Khaya, is about 2,960 m high.
Oymyakon, one of the coldest inhabited places on Earth, lies to the north of the range.

q.q: Which village, famous for extreme cold, lies near the Suntar-Khayata?

Q1557099.t: Remote ridges above a field of summer ice
Q1557099.s: A white field of ice lying in green tundra in midsummer: that is the Moma aufeis, one of the largest in the world, built up each winter as seeping river and ground water freezes layer upon layer. Above it rise the Momsky mountains, bare grey ridges running for hundreds of kilometres through north-eastern Yakutia, almost untouched by people.
Q1557099.w: Bare grey ridges running north-west to south-east in north-eastern Yakutia, parallel to the higher Chersky Range to the south-west.
f: An aufeis forms when water seeps out onto river ice in winter and freezes in thick layers.
The Moma River flows between the Momsky and Chersky ranges into the Indigirka.

q.q: What is an aufeis, like the one in the Moma valley?

Q11948856.t: Bare ridges named after a surprising language
Q11948856.s: South of Quetta, Balochistan's ridges run in long, parallel folds of bare rock, grey and ochre under a hard sun. These are the Central Brahui Ranges, named after the Brahui people. Their language is one of the great puzzles of linguistics: it belongs to the Dravidian family, whose other members are spoken mainly in southern India, well over a thousand kilometres away.
Q11948856.w: Long, parallel folds of bare grey and ochre rock running north–south around the town of Kalat, south of Quetta.
f: Brahui is a Dravidian language, related to Tamil and Telugu.
These folded ridges were pushed up as the Indian plate collided with Eurasia.

q.q: To which language family does Brahui belong?

Q2062939.t: The 'black mountains' reaching into the Kazakh steppe
Q2062939.s: Karatau means 'black mountains', and the ridges do look dark against the pale steppe around them. This long arm of the Tian Shan pushes some 400 km north-west into southern Kazakhstan. Its rocks hold rich phosphate deposits and a famous Jurassic lake bed full of fossil insects. At its south-western foot lies Turkistan, an ancient Silk Road city.
Q2062939.w: A long, dark ridge running north-west into the pale steppe, with the Syr Darya valley and the city of Turkistan to the south-west.
f: The mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi in Turkistan is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
The range holds large phosphorite deposits, mined for fertiliser.
Fossil insects from Karatau's Jurassic lake beds, about 160 million years old, are studied worldwide.

q.q: What does the Turkic name Karatau mean?

Q784189.t: A 'Throne of Solomon' above the Indus plain
Q784189.s: West of the Indus, the flat green plain of Punjab ends against a long wall of bare, folded rock: the Sulaiman Mountains. They run for hundreds of kilometres north to south, brown and ochre, with snow on the highest crests in winter. Their best-known summit, Takht-e-Sulaiman, about 3,500 m high, is the 'Throne of Solomon', tied by legend to the biblical king.
Q784189.w: A long north–south wall of bare brown ridges rising abruptly from the green Indus plain to the east.
f: Takht-e-Sulaiman means 'Throne of Solomon'.
Dera Ghazi Khan lies on the plain at the range's eastern foot.
Flash floods from its dry valleys spread wide fans of gravel onto the Indus plain.

q.q: What does the name Takht-e-Sulaiman mean?

Q5061389.t: Combed ridges where Alexander's army suffered
Q5061389.s: From above, the Makran looks combed: long, parallel ridges of bare rock, grey, tan and pink, separated by dry valleys. The Central Makran Range runs east–west through southern Balochistan, part of a vast belt of folds pushed up as the Arabian Sea floor slides beneath Asia. In 325 BC Alexander the Great led his army back from India across this land, at a terrible cost.
Q5061389.w: Parallel, striped ridges of bare rock running east–west, with narrow valleys between them, inland from the Arabian Sea coast.
f: The ancient Greeks called this dry coastland Gedrosia.
The Makran folds rise above a zone where the Arabian plate dives beneath Eurasia.

q.q: Which ancient conqueror crossed the Makran desert in 325 BC?

Q2140102.t: Wild goats on a dry rampart above the Indus
Q2140102.s: The Kirthar Mountains form a clean edge: to the east, the flat, irrigated Indus plain of Sindh; to the west, rank after rank of bare, tilted ridges. They run north–south for roughly 300 km along the boundary of Sindh and Balochistan. Rain is scarce, yet the range shelters wild goats, urial sheep and one of Pakistan's largest national parks.
Q2140102.w: Bare, tilted brown ridges running north–south, with the flat green strip of the Indus plain along their eastern side.
f: Kirthar National Park, created in 1974, protects Sindh ibex and urial.
Gorakh Hill, at about 1,700 m, is one of the highest points in Sindh.

q.q: Which river's plain lies east of the Kirthar Mountains?

Q328072.t: A long fence between the Karakum and the Iranian plateau
Q328072.s: The Kopet Dag rises like a fence between two worlds: to the north, the sands of the Karakum Desert; to the south, the high Iranian plateau. For some 600 km its folded ridges run north-west to south-east, and along the northern foot grew a string of oases fed by mountain springs. Ashgabat, Turkmenistan's white-marble capital, sits right against the range.
Q328072.w: A long, straight line of folded brown ridges, with the flat Karakum Desert to the north and Ashgabat at their foot.
f: The ruins of Nisa, an early Parthian capital near Ashgabat, are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Akhal-Teke horses, famed for their metallic sheen, were bred in the oases at its foot.

q.q: Which desert lies north of the Kopet Dag?

Q172556.t: Snowy limestone peaks above Turkey's Riviera
Q172556.s: Behind Turkey's Mediterranean coast rises a long barrier of limestone: the Taurus Mountains, curving for hundreds of kilometres from Antalya towards the Euphrates. Their bare grey peaks hold snow into early summer, and deep gorges cut down to the sea. For millennia a narrow pass, the Cilician Gates, linked Anatolia with the Levant; Alexander the Great marched through it in 333 BC.
Q172556.w: Grey limestone ridges with snowy crests running parallel to Turkey's southern coast, between the blue Mediterranean and the Anatolian plateau.
f: The Cilician Gates pass lies north of the city of Tarsus.
The Tigris rises in the Eastern Taurus.
The highest summits, in the Aladağlar massif, reach about 3,750 m.

q.q: Which pass through the Taurus did Alexander the Great use?

Q11748964.t: The Carpathians' granite crown beyond green Beskid ridges
Q11748964.s: Along the Polish–Slovak border, soft green ridges of the Beskids roll one behind another, covered in spruce and beech. Further east the land suddenly hardens into the Tatras: a compact block of grey granite peaks, streaked with snow and dotted with glacial lakes. Gerlachovský štít, 2,655 m, in the Slovak Tatras, is the highest point of the entire Carpathian arc.
Q11748964.w: Rolling forested ridges near the Czech–Polish–Slovak borders, rising further east into a compact cluster of bare grey peaks.
f: Rysy, about 2,500 m, is Poland's highest mountain.
Morskie Oko is the best known of the Tatras' many glacial lakes.
Babia Góra, about 1,725 m, is the highest summit of the Western Beskids.

q.q: What is the highest peak of the Tatras and the whole Carpathians?

Q201582.t: The rocky backbone of mainland Greece
Q201582.s: The Pindus runs down the middle of northern Greece like a backbone, separating Epirus from Thessaly. Its limestone and dark ophiolite ridges hide some of Europe's wildest country, where brown bears and wolves still live. Here too is the Vikos Gorge, famous for its depth compared with its width. On the range's eastern edge, the rock towers of Meteora carry monasteries on their tops.
Q201582.w: A long, rugged north–south ridge through northern Greece, with the flat Thessaly plain to the east and Ioannina's lake to the west.
f: Smolikas, about 2,640 m, is Greece's second-highest mountain after Olympus.
Guinness World Records has listed the Vikos Gorge as the deepest gorge relative to its width.

q.q: Which monasteries stand on rock towers at the edge of the Pindus?

Q3658589.t: A cold, wet plateau rising from the boreal forest
Q3658589.s: In the far north of Alberta, a broad plateau rises several hundred metres above endless boreal lowlands. The Caribou Mountains are not peaks at all but a high tableland of lakes and bogs, cold enough that patches of permafrost survive under the peat, far south of the true Arctic. Woodland caribou, which gave the range its name, still roam its spruce and lichen.
Q3658589.w: A broad raised plateau speckled with small lakes and bogs in northern Alberta, north of the Peace River.
f: Much of the plateau is protected as the Caribou Mountains Wildland Provincial Park.
Wood Buffalo National Park, the largest in Canada, lies to the east.

q.q: What survives under the bogs of the Caribou Mountains?

Q283784.t: Dark granite spires on the road to the Arctic
Q283784.s: North of Dawson City, the Dempster Highway climbs into the Ogilvie Mountains, and the only road in the region becomes a thin gravel thread through the tundra. The most striking peaks stand in Tombstone Territorial Park, where black granite spires rise above green valleys and rust-red slopes. In September the tundra turns scarlet and gold, one of the great autumn shows of the north.
Q283784.w: Rugged grey and black peaks with tundra valleys north of the Yukon River, crossed by a single gravel road heading north.
f: The mountains are named after William Ogilvie, a Canadian surveyor of the Klondike era.
The Dempster Highway runs about 740 km from near Dawson City to Inuvik.
Tombstone Mountain takes its name from its dark, slab-like summit.

q.q: Which road crosses the Ogilvie Mountains towards the Arctic?

Q616559.t: Giant volcanoes in America's largest national park
Q616559.s: The Wrangells are volcanoes on a colossal scale: broad, ice-covered giants rising above 4,000 m from the Copper River basin. Mount Wrangell, a vast shield volcano, still vents steam near its summit, while Mount Blackburn, the highest at about 5,000 m, is one of the tallest volcanoes in the United States. All of it lies within Wrangell–St. Elias, the country's largest national park.
Q616559.w: Massive ice-capped domes rising above a broad river basin, with long glaciers spreading from their flanks, east of the Copper River.
f: Wrangell–St. Elias National Park covers about 53,000 km², more than Switzerland.
The abandoned Kennecott copper mines lie at the southern foot of the range.
Mount Wrangell has an ice-filled caldera at its summit.

q.q: Which is the largest national park in the United States?

Q166755.t: Ridge behind ridge, fading into blue haze
Q166755.s: On a summer day the Blue Ridge looks exactly like its name: ridge behind ridge, each a paler shade of blue until they merge with the sky. The haze comes partly from natural compounds released by the dense forests. These old, rounded mountains are part of the Appalachians and hold Mount Mitchell, 2,037 m, the highest summit east of the Mississippi.
Q166755.w: Layer upon layer of rounded, forested ridges in shades of blue, running north-east to south-west through the southern Appalachians.
f: The Blue Ridge Parkway winds for about 755 km along the mountains.
Great Smoky Mountains National Park, in the Blue Ridge, is the most visited national park in the United States.
Much of the blue haze comes from isoprene, a gas given off by trees.

q.q: Which is the highest peak east of the Mississippi?

Q1744263.t: A tangle of ancient ocean crust beside Mount Shasta
Q1744263.s: West of Mount Shasta's white cone, the land breaks into a tangle of steep, forested ridges with no obvious pattern: the Klamath Mountains. Unlike the young volcanoes next door, they are built from ancient slices of ocean crust and island arcs pushed onto the continent. Wild rivers such as the Klamath and the Trinity cut deep canyons through them, and their forests are famous for their many kinds of conifer.
Q1744263.w: A jumble of dark green, steep ridges between the snowy cone of Mount Shasta and the Pacific coast, on the California–Oregon border.
f: The range includes the Trinity Alps, the Siskiyou Mountains and the Marble Mountains.
Serpentine rock from the old sea floor supports unusual plants found almost nowhere else.

q.q: Which snowy volcano rises just east of the Klamath Mountains?

Q2033447.t: Rare east–west ridges in the heart of America
Q2033447.s: Most American mountain ranges run roughly north–south, but the Ouachitas break the rule. Their long, forested ridges run east to west across western Arkansas and south-eastern Oklahoma, like parallel waves frozen in stone. They were folded up some 300 million years ago. At their eastern end, springs at the town of Hot Springs bring water to the surface at over 60 °C.
Q2033447.w: Long, parallel forested ridges running east–west, with reservoirs in the valleys, west of Little Rock.
f: The Ouachitas are known for their clear quartz crystals.
The hot springs at their eastern edge were set aside as a federal reservation in 1832.

q.q: In which direction do the Ouachita ridges run?

Q7405538.t: Deep canyons around the 'River of No Return'
Q7405538.s: Central Idaho is a sea of forested ridges, and the Salmon River Mountains sit at its heart, cut by some of the deepest canyons in North America. The Salmon River loops around them in a gorge that earned it the name 'River of No Return': early boats could float down but not come back up. Much of the range lies inside the largest wilderness area in the lower 48 states.
Q7405538.w: A maze of steep, forested ridges and deep, twisting canyons in central Idaho, with almost no roads.
f: The Frank Church–River of No Return Wilderness covers about 9,600 km².
The Middle Fork of the Salmon is one of the classic whitewater rivers of the United States.

q.q: What nickname does the Salmon River carry?

Q186910.t: The long cliff edge of the Colorado Plateau
Q186910.s: Here the Colorado Plateau simply stops. The Mogollon Rim is an escarpment running some 300 km across central Arizona, with cliffs and steep slopes dropping hundreds of metres to the lower desert country around Payson. On top spreads one of the largest ponderosa pine forests on Earth; below, the land turns to scrub and cactus. The line between the two is sharp.
Q186910.w: A long, dark-green forested edge with a steep drop to the south, running north-west to south-east across central Arizona.
f: The rim is named after Juan Ignacio Flores Mogollón, an 18th-century Spanish governor of New Mexico.
Novelist Zane Grey set several westerns on the rim, where he kept a cabin.

q.q: Which tree dominates the forests on top of the Mogollon Rim?

Q931210.t: The Andes' last high branch, between lake and plains
Q931210.s: The Andes make their final high push in Venezuela. The Cordillera de Mérida slants north-east for some 400 km, separating the hot basin of Lake Maracaibo from the grassy Llanos. Its crest carries the country's only peaks near 5,000 m, and below them spread the páramos: cold, wet moors of small lakes and silver-leaved frailejón plants.
Q931210.w: A long, high ridge slanting north-east, with the vast blue Lake Maracaibo on one side and flat green plains on the other.
f: Its three highest summits, Pico Bolívar, Humboldt and Bonpland, all rise above 4,800 m.
The city of Mérida lies deep inside the range, in the valley of the Chama River.

q.q: Which huge lake lies west of the Cordillera de Mérida?

Q1143026.t: A gentle 'knife' ridge across Uruguay's grasslands
Q1143026.s: Uruguay has no real mountains, only long, gentle ridges that locals call cuchillas, 'knives'. The Cuchilla Grande is the main one, running north-east through the east of the country towards Brazil. From the air it is barely a ripple: rolling green pasture, grey rock outcrops, lines of eucalyptus and scattered cattle ranches. Its highest point, Cerro Catedral, is only about 514 m.
Q1143026.w: Low, grassy, undulating hills with rocky outcrops and eucalyptus stands, running north-east through eastern Uruguay.
f: Cerro Catedral, about 514 m, is the highest point of Uruguay.
Uruguay has roughly three times as many cattle as people.

q.q: What does the Spanish word cuchilla literally mean?

Q2120979.t: Rainforest mountains named after a Dutch queen
Q2120979.s: Almost nothing but forest surrounds the Wilhelmina Mountains, a line of granite ridges rising from the unbroken green canopy of central Suriname. Their highest point, Julianatop, a little over 1,200 m, is also the highest point in the country. The whole area lies within the Central Suriname Nature Reserve, one of the largest stretches of untouched tropical forest on Earth.
Q2120979.w: Dark green forested ridges rising above an unbroken sea of rainforest in the centre of Suriname, with no roads or clearings.
f: The range is named after Queen Wilhelmina of the Netherlands, and Julianatop after her daughter Juliana.
The Central Suriname Nature Reserve, about 16,000 km², became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2000.

q.q: Julianatop is the highest point of which country?

Q3621380.t: Forest hills where the Essequibo is born
Q3621380.s: On the southern edge of Guyana, along the border with Brazil, a line of forested hills forms a watershed deep in the rainforest. The Acarai Mountains are modest in height, but they matter: from their northern slopes flows the Essequibo, Guyana's greatest river, while streams on the southern side run towards the Amazon. The green canopy continues unbroken in every direction.
Q3621380.w: Low, forest-covered hills along the Guyana–Brazil border, with the green canopy stretching unbroken in every direction.
f: The Essequibo, which rises here, is Guyana's longest river, about 1,000 km long.
The Wai-Wai people live in the forests near the river's headwaters.

q.q: Which river rises in the Acarai Mountains?

Q5761832.t: A sandstone plateau of savanna in the rainforest
Q5761832.s: Pale patches of savanna break the dark rainforest here, marking the Serra do Cachimbo. The soils of this broad sandstone plateau in southern Pará are so poor and sandy that the forest gives way to open grassland and scrub. Rivers drain from it towards the Tapajós and the Xingu, and the long Cuiabá–Santarém highway crosses its back.
Q5761832.w: Paler patches of open savanna and bare sandstone amid dark rainforest in southern Pará, crossed by a north–south highway.
f: The BR-163 highway, linking Cuiabá with Santarém on the Amazon, crosses the plateau.
Its sandy soils support savanna vegetation, unusual in the middle of the rainforest.

q.q: What vegetation covers much of the Cachimbo plateau?

Q22024985.t: Cerrado highlands between Brasília and Goiânia
Q22024985.s: Brazil's high central plateau rises here into ridges and flat-topped tablelands about 1,000 m above sea level. This is cerrado country: a savanna of twisted trees and grass, now largely broken up by vast rectangles of soy and cattle pasture, with red earth showing between them. Not far away, near Brasília, the rain divides between three of South America's great river basins.
Q22024985.w: Red earth, rectangular fields and patches of scrubby savanna on a high plateau between Brasília and Goiânia.
f: The cerrado is considered the most species-rich savanna on Earth.
Near Brasília, the Águas Emendadas wetland feeds the Tocantins, Paraná and São Francisco basins.

q.q: What is the savanna of Brazil's central plateau called?

Q766931.t: A rugged peninsula beside the Pacific's highest tides
Q766931.s: At the top of the Sea of Okhotsk, the Taygonos Peninsula juts south between two long bays like a clenched fist of mountains. On its eastern side lies Penzhina Bay, where the tides are the highest in the whole Pacific, rising and falling by more than ten metres. The peninsula itself is roadless and almost uninhabited: bare ridges, tundra and, in winter, ice-choked shores.
Q766931.w: A mountainous peninsula pointing south into the northern Sea of Okhotsk, between two long, narrow bays.
f: Tides in Penzhina Bay can reach about 13 m, the highest in the Pacific Ocean.
The peninsula separates Gizhiga Bay from Penzhina Bay, both arms of Shelikhov Gulf.

q.q: Which bay beside Taygonos has the Pacific's highest tides?

Q893152.t: Where the magnetic north pole was first found
Q893152.s: In June 1831 James Clark Ross stood on the west coast of this peninsula and watched his compass needle point almost straight down: he had reached the North Magnetic Pole. The pole has since wandered far away, but Boothia still holds a record of its own. Its northern tip is the northernmost point of mainland North America.
Q893152.w: A broad, tundra-covered peninsula reaching north into the Arctic channels, joined to the mainland by a narrow neck of land.
f: It is named after Felix Booth, a London gin distiller who funded the expedition.
Its northern tip, on Murchison Promontory, lies at almost 72° N.
The magnetic pole has since drifted across the Arctic Ocean towards Siberia.

q.q: Who located the North Magnetic Pole on Boothia in 1831?

Q60010.t: Icefield, fjords and salmon rivers south of Anchorage
Q60010.s: Just south of Anchorage, the Kenai Peninsula packs much of Alaska into one view. Its eastern half is buried under the Harding Icefield, which sends dozens of glaciers down towards the sea, many ending in the fjords of Kenai Fjords National Park. The western half is lower, dotted with lakes and crossed by the turquoise Kenai River, famous for its giant salmon.
Q60010.w: A large peninsula south of Anchorage: a broad white icefield on the eastern side, lake-dotted lowlands along Cook Inlet in the west.
f: The Harding Icefield covers about 1,800 km².
The world-record king salmon, about 44 kg, was caught in the Kenai River in 1985.
The peninsula takes its name from the Kenaitze, a Dena'ina people.

q.q: Which icefield covers much of the Kenai Peninsula?

Q971586.t: America's tip, facing Asia across the Bering Strait
Q971586.s: The Seward Peninsula is where America reaches out towards Asia. Its western tip, Cape Prince of Wales, is the westernmost point of the mainland Americas, only about 82 km from Russia's Chukchi Peninsula across the Bering Strait. In the ice ages the sea floor here was dry land, the Bering Land Bridge, the route by which the first people are thought to have reached the Americas.
Q971586.w: A broad, treeless peninsula of tundra and low mountains pointing west towards the narrow Bering Strait.
f: It is named after William Seward, the US Secretary of State who arranged the purchase of Alaska in 1867.
A gold rush brought thousands of prospectors to the beaches of Nome in 1899–1900.
Bering Land Bridge National Preserve protects part of the peninsula.

q.q: What is Cape Prince of Wales, the tip of the Seward Peninsula?

Q850245.t: The water tower of West Africa
Q850245.s: Much of West Africa's water starts here. The Fouta Djallon is a highland of sandstone plateaus in Guinea, cut by deep valleys and waterfalls, and its heavy rains feed the headwaters of the Senegal and Gambia rivers, among others. Its flat-topped tablelands end in sheer cliffs, with forest in the valleys and bare, rust-coloured rock on top.
Q850245.w: Flat-topped sandstone tablelands with sheer edges and green valleys in central Guinea, inland from the Atlantic coast.
f: The Bafing, the main headstream of the Senegal River, rises here.
In the 18th century the Fula people founded a Muslim state here, the Imamate of Futa Jallon.
Mount Loura, one of its highest summits, reaches about 1,500 m.

q.q: Which major river rises in the Fouta Djallon?

Q1462530.t: The 'great barrier' of sandstone in the empty Sahara
Q1462530.s: In Egypt's far south-western corner, a vast sandstone plateau rises some 300 m above the desert. Gilf Kebir means 'great barrier', and its sheer, dark cliffs are cut by valleys choked with golden sand. In a shallow cave on its edge, the Hungarian explorer László Almásy found paintings of people who seem to be swimming, made when the Sahara was green.
Q1462530.w: A dark, cliff-edged plateau with sand-filled valleys, rising from pale desert near the corner where Egypt, Libya and Sudan meet.
f: Almásy found the Cave of Swimmers in 1933.
The cave appears in the novel and film 'The English Patient'.
The plateau became part of Gilf Kebir National Park in 2007.

q.q: What does the Arabic name Gilf Kebir mean?

Q755509.t: A green volcanic tableland above the reef coast
Q755509.s: Climb west from Cairns and the rainforest opens onto a rolling green plateau of dairy farms, volcanic cones and deep crater lakes. The Atherton Tableland lies mostly between about 600 and 1,000 m, cooler and gentler than the steamy coast below. Its rich red volcanic soils grow crops from avocados to coffee, and pockets of rainforest shelter tree-kangaroos.
Q755509.w: A rolling green plateau with small round lakes and patches of dark forest, just inland from Cairns and the reef coast.
f: Lake Eacham and Lake Barrine fill craters left by explosive volcanic eruptions.
The rainforests around it belong to the Wet Tropics of Queensland World Heritage site.

q.q: Which kangaroo lives in the rainforests of the Atherton Tableland?

Q1414064.t: The Volga's high right bank, hundreds of kilometres long
Q1414064.s: Along the Volga, one bank is high and the other low, and the Volga Upland is the high one. From near Nizhny Novgorod down to Volgograd it rises on the river's western side as a broad, gullied plateau of chalk, clay and limestone, sometimes ending in pale cliffs above the water. At the Samara Bend the Volga loops around the forested Zhiguli Mountains, the upland's most dramatic corner.
Q1414064.w: A broad upland of fields and wooded ravines along the western bank of the Volga, with the wide river and its reservoirs to the east.
f: The Zhiguli Mountains in the Samara Bend are protected as a nature reserve and a national park.
Ulyanovsk and Saratov stand on the upland's edge above the Volga.

q.q: Which mountains does the Volga loop around at the Samara Bend?

Q906924.t: Granite and black earth on the Dnieper's high bank
Q906924.s: Some of the most fertile soil on Earth covers this upland. West of the Dnieper the land rolls gently, cut by deep river valleys, and beneath its thick black chernozem lies the granite of the Ukrainian Shield, one of Europe's oldest rock foundations. The granite breaks through in rapids and small canyons on rivers such as the Southern Bug, amid a vast patchwork of fields and tree lines.
Q906924.w: A gently rolling plain of large fields and wooded ravines west of the Dnieper, with rivers cutting narrow valleys into it.
f: In places the black chernozem here is more than a metre thick.
The poet Taras Shevchenko is buried on a hill above the Dnieper at Kaniv, on the upland's eastern edge.
The granite beneath is well over 1.5 billion years old.

q.q: What is the region's famous black soil called?

Q190695.t: France's volcanic heartland of old, worn mountains
Q190695.s: A line of some 80 neat volcanic cones, the Chaîne des Puys, marks the northern part of the Massif Central. This great block of old, worn-down mountains and high plateaus covers about 15% of France. Further south lie bare granite uplands, deep gorges and limestone causses, and the Loire and many other rivers begin here.
Q190695.w: A broad upland of rounded hills, high plateaus and volcanic cones in south-central France, between the Rhône valley and Toulouse.
f: The Chaîne des Puys and the Limagne fault became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2018.
The Puy de Sancy, about 1,885 m, is the highest point of the Massif Central.
The Loire, France's longest river, rises on the slopes of Mont Gerbier de Jonc.

q.q: Which river rises at Mont Gerbier de Jonc in the Massif Central?

Q5072889.t: A flat-topped table packed with Cretaceous fossils
Q5072889.s: Rising from the dry scrub of north-eastern Brazil, the Chapada do Araripe is a long plateau with a dead-flat top and steep edges, like a table laid across the backlands. Its rock layers are one of the world's great fossil treasuries, holding exquisitely preserved fish, insects and pterosaurs from the Cretaceous. Springs at its foot keep the cities of Crato and Juazeiro do Norte green.
Q5072889.w: A long plateau with a flat top and steep edges, rising above dry scrubland on the Ceará–Pernambuco border.
f: Araripe became the first UNESCO Global Geopark in the Americas in 2006.
The Araripe manakin, a small bird with a red crest, lives only at the foot of this plateau.
Many of its fossils come from the Santana Formation, over 100 million years old.
