q.q: What is the Chapada do Araripe famous for?

Q141513.t: One of the hottest, lowest, strangest places on Earth
Q141513.s: The Danakil is where Africa is slowly tearing apart. Parts of this desert lie more than 100 m below sea level, and it is one of the hottest places on the planet. In its depths, the hot springs of Dallol paint the salt in acid yellows and greens, and the volcano Erta Ale is famous for its long-lived lava lake. Afar camel caravans still carry slabs of salt out of the basin.
Q141513.w: A vast pale basin of salt flats and dark lava fields near the Red Sea coast, in the Horn of Africa.
f: The Danakil lies at a junction of three rifts pulling the crust apart.
Dallol holds the record for the highest average temperature measured at an inhabited place.
Salt has been cut from these flats and carried away by camel for centuries.

q.q: Which volcano in the Danakil is famous for its lava lake?

Q23782559.t: A stony plateau where the Sahara has no sand
Q23782559.s: Not all of the Sahara is sand. The Hamada de Tinrhert is a vast stony plateau near the Algeria–Libya border, swept by wind until only flat rock and a pavement of dark pebbles remain. To the north lie the dunes of the Grand Erg Oriental; to the south the land climbs towards the Tassili n'Ajjer. It looks like dark, wrinkled leather laid across the desert.
Q23782559.w: A dark, flat stony plateau cut by a few dry valleys, between orange dunes to the north and rocky highlands to the south.
f: Hamada is the Arabic term for a bare, rocky desert plateau.
The dark sheen on its stones is desert varnish, a thin coating of iron and manganese oxides.

q.q: What is a hamada?

Q1350167.t: Red dune ridges named after a Polish explorer
Q1350167.s: Long red sand ridges run side by side for tens of kilometres here, like combed hair, with pale clay pans in the hollows between them. The Strzelecki Desert spreads across the corner where South Australia, Queensland and New South Wales meet. It is named after the Polish explorer Paweł Strzelecki, best remembered for climbing and naming Australia's highest mountain, Mount Kosciuszko.
Q1350167.w: Parallel red dune ridges with white clay pans between them, in the far north-east of South Australia.
f: Strzelecki named Mount Kosciuszko in 1840 after the Polish-Lithuanian hero Tadeusz Kościuszko.
The Dog Fence, one of the longest fences in the world, crosses this corner of Australia.
The Moomba gas fields lie within the desert.

q.q: Which mountain did Paweł Strzelecki name?

Q211839.t: A thousand red dunes marching in parallel lines
Q211839.s: Crossing the Simpson Desert by track means climbing over roughly 1,100 sand dunes, one after another. From the air they form an astonishing pattern: long, straight red ridges running north-north-west for tens of kilometres, parallel like the grooves of a record, with pale clay flats in between. The desert covers some 170,000 km² in the heart of Australia, north of Lake Eyre.
Q211839.w: Endless parallel red dune ridges running north-north-west, with white salt or clay pans between them, north of Lake Eyre.
f: Big Red, or Nappanerica, the best-known dune, stands about 40 m high.
It is named after Alfred Simpson, an Adelaide businessman who funded its aerial survey in 1929.
It is often described as the world's largest parallel dune desert.

q.q: Roughly how many dunes does a west–east crossing of the Simpson involve?

Q674262.t: Red sandplains and spinifex in Australia's empty north
Q674262.s: The Tanami is less about towering dunes than endless flat red sand, speckled with grey-green hummocks of spinifex grass and scattered termite mounds. It spreads across the Northern Territory and into Western Australia, crossed by one long dirt road, the Tanami Track. After rare heavy rains temporary lakes appear, and the red earth turns briefly green.
Q674262.w: Vast flat red plains with a grey-green speckle of spinifex, occasional low ridges and white salt lakes, north-west of Alice Springs.
f: The Tanami Track runs about 1,000 km from near Alice Springs to Halls Creek.
The desert is the traditional country of the Warlpiri people, among others.

q.q: Which spiky grass covers much of the Tanami Desert?

Q2088454.t: A rust-red sea of dunes in southern Afghanistan
Q2088454.s: Iron oxide paints this desert the colour of rust. The Registan, whose Persian name means 'land of sand', spreads south of Kandahar as a plateau of dunes tens of metres high, in shades from orange to deep red. Along its western edge, the Helmand River draws a green line of irrigated fields through the sand, a vivid stripe against the red.
Q2088454.w: A broad field of rust-red dunes south of Kandahar, with the green ribbon of the Helmand valley along its western edge.
f: Registan means 'land of sand' in Persian.
The Helmand, Afghanistan's longest river, skirts the desert's western edge.

q.q: What does the Persian name Registan mean?

Q2356478.t: The 'Desert of Death' between two rivers
Q2356478.s: Its name, Dasht-e Margo, means 'desert of death', and from above it is easy to see why: a vast expanse of wind-scoured clay, gravel and low dunes in south-western Afghanistan, with barely a track across it. Two rivers frame it, the Helmand along its southern side and the Khash Rud to the north. Both end in the marshy Sistan basin on the Iranian border.
Q2356478.w: A vast pale expanse of clay flats, gravel and low dunes, bordered by the green thread of the Helmand valley to the south.
f: In Persian, dasht means 'plain' or 'desert' and marg means 'death'.
The Helmand and the Khash Rud both run out into the lakes and marshes of the Sistan basin.

q.q: What does the name Dasht-e Margo mean?

Q272514.t: Iran's great salt desert, a crust over hidden mud
Q272514.s: Its glittering crust of salt hides treacherous mud, which is why caravans always kept to its edges. The Dasht-e Kavir, Iran's Great Salt Desert, covers roughly 77,000 km² in the heart of the Iranian plateau. It looks like frosted glass, streaked with brown where old stream channels and patches of clay break the white.
Q272514.w: A huge, pale, salt-crusted basin in north-central Iran, south-east of Tehran, fringed by brown hills.
f: Kavir is the Persian word for a salt marsh.
Old caravanserais, such as Maranjab, stand on its fringes along former trade routes.

q.q: Why did caravans keep to the edges of the Dasht-e Kavir?
q.a: Its salt crust hides soft mud

Q749205.t: Brick-red dunes above ancient rock art
Q749205.s: The Great Nafud is famous for the colour of its sand, a deep brick red from iron oxide, and for its huge crescent-shaped dunes, carved and recarved by strong winds. It fills a broad basin in northern Saudi Arabia. On its southern edge, around the oasis of Jubbah, the rocks carry thousands of carvings of people and animals made over thousands of years.
Q749205.w: A broad oval of red sand dunes in northern Saudi Arabia, north of the city of Ha'il.
f: The rock art of Jubbah and Shuwaymis became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2015.
Its sand owes its red colour to a thin coating of iron oxide.

q.q: What gives the Nafud's sand its red colour?

Q574853.t: Morocco's oldest rocks, bare and coloured like spice
Q574853.s: Around the town of Tafraoute, pink granite boulders pile up like giant marbles. South of the High Atlas, Morocco's mountains grow older and barer: the Anti-Atlas is built from some of the most ancient rocks in North Africa, folded and worn into ridges of ochre, pink and purple, with few trees except argan. Villages of earth-coloured houses cling to the slopes.
Q574853.w: Bare, colourful ridges of ochre and purple rock south of the snowy High Atlas, fading south-west towards the Atlantic and east into the Sahara.
f: The argan tree, source of argan oil, grows naturally almost only in south-western Morocco.
Taliouine, near the volcanic Jbel Siroua, is known as Morocco's saffron capital.
Some of its rocks are about 2 billion years old.

q.q: Which tree, source of a prized oil, grows wild on the Anti-Atlas slopes?

Q22071997.t: The 'mountains that weep' above south-east Brazil
Q22071997.s: Mantiqueira is often said to mean 'mountains that weep' in Tupi, and the name fits: countless springs and waterfalls pour off these granite heights between São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais. The range climbs to nearly 2,800 m, with rocky summits above highland grassland, and cool towns such as Campos do Jordão draw visitors escaping the tropical heat.
Q22071997.w: A long line of dark granite ridges and grassy highlands running north-east, between the Paraíba valley and the hills of southern Minas Gerais.
f: Itatiaia, in the Mantiqueira, became Brazil's first national park in 1937.
Its highest summits, Pedra da Mina and Agulhas Negras, both reach about 2,790 m.

q.q: Which was Brazil's first national park, created in 1937?

Q27036.t: Cloud forests above the Pacific coast of Chiapas
Q27036.s: Along Mexico's southern Pacific coast, a steep wall of mountains rises from a narrow plain of mango and banana plantations. The Sierra Madre de Chiapas climbs quickly into cloud forest, where the resplendent quetzal still lives, and coffee grows in the shade on its slopes. At its south-eastern end stands Tacaná, a volcano over 4,000 m high on the border with Guatemala.
Q27036.w: A steep, dark-green mountain wall parallel to the Pacific coast, with a narrow coastal plain between it and the sea.
f: The El Triunfo Biosphere Reserve protects cloud forest home to quetzals and horned guans.
The Soconusco coffee region lies on its Pacific slopes.
Tacaná volcano is about 4,060 m high.

q.q: Which famous bird lives in the cloud forests of this range?

Q7448930.t: Wild peaks on the divide between two great rivers
Q7448930.s: The Selwyn Mountains form a rugged, little-visited wilderness along the border of Yukon and the Northwest Territories. Their grey, glacier-carved peaks and green valleys roughly follow a great divide: water on the western side flows to the Yukon River and the Bering Sea, while on the eastern side it heads for the Mackenzie and the Arctic Ocean. Roads barely touch them.
Q7448930.w: Jagged grey peaks with small glaciers and long green valleys along the Yukon–Northwest Territories border.
f: They are named after Alfred Selwyn, an early director of the Geological Survey of Canada.
The Yukon–Northwest Territories border here roughly follows the drainage divide.

q.q: Where do rivers from the east side of the Selwyn Mountains flow?

Q5644542.t: Korea's second-highest summit on a snowy coastal ridge
Q5644542.s: Only one mountain in Korea stands higher than Kwanmobong, the crown of the Hamgyong range. These mountains form a long wall in the far north-east of the peninsula, rising steeply from the coast and sloping more gently inland. Kwanmobong, about 2,540 m, is second only to Paektu. In winter the crest turns white early, and larch and fir forests cover the lower slopes.
Q5644542.w: A long, high ridge running north-east to south-west close to the coast, snowy in winter, with forested valleys inland.
f: Kwanmobong, about 2,540 m, is the second-highest mountain on the Korean Peninsula.
Mount Chilbo, a scenic area of strange rock pillars, lies near the coast east of the range.

q.q: Which is the only Korean peak higher than Kwanmobong?

Q1429556.s: Kamchatka has two mountain chains, and the Sredinny Range is the inner one, running for some 900 km down the middle of the peninsula. Its crest is a string of old volcanoes and snowy ridges, crowned by Ichinsky, about 3,600 m, a volcano that still has steaming vents. In the valleys lie hot springs and villages such as Esso, warmed by heat from deep underground.
Q1429556.w: A long, snowy spine down the middle of Kamchatka, with a broad river valley separating it from the volcanoes of the east coast.
f: Ichinsky volcano, about 3,600 m, is the highest point of the range.
The village of Esso is heated by water from hot springs.
Bystrinsky Nature Park, in the range, is part of the 'Volcanoes of Kamchatka' UNESCO site.

q.q: What heats the village of Esso in the Sredinny Range?

Q644145.t: Treeless mountains on the Bering Sea coast
Q644145.s: Fog rolls in from the Bering Sea over mountains with hardly a tree on them. The Koryak Highlands run for hundreds of kilometres between Kamchatka and Chukotka, rugged and bare, with small glaciers on the highest peaks and tundra in the valleys. Few people live here beyond scattered coastal villages and Koryak reindeer herders.
Q644145.w: A broad band of bare, rugged ridges with small glaciers along the Bering Sea coast, north-east of Kamchatka.
f: The highest point, Mount Ledyanaya, whose name means 'icy', is about 2,500 m high.
The mountains are named after the Koryak people, traditional reindeer herders and sea hunters.

q.q: Which sea washes the coast of the Koryak Mountains?

Q1245603.t: The watershed between the Kolyma and the Pacific
Q1245603.s: A raindrop falling here may end up in the Arctic Ocean or in the Pacific, depending on which side of the ridge it lands. The Kolyma Mountains run north-east from Magadan towards Chukotka, a sea of bare, rounded summits and steep-sided valleys that divides the Kolyma basin from rivers flowing south. For most of the year this is a white, silent land of snow and sparse larch.
Q1245603.w: Endless bare, rounded summits and narrow valleys with thin larch forest, stretching from Magadan's hinterland towards Chukotka.
f: The Omolon, a major tributary of the Kolyma, rises in these mountains.
Winter temperatures below −40 °C are common here.

q.q: Into which ocean does the Kolyma River carry its water?

Q683923.t: A 1,500-km range named after a Polish exile
Q683923.s: The Chersky Range sweeps some 1,500 km across north-eastern Siberia, a maze of sharp grey ridges, small glaciers and gorges. It was mapped properly only in the 1920s, when geologist Sergei Obruchev named it after Jan Czerski, a Polish exile who had explored the region decades earlier. The Indigirka River cuts right through it in deep canyons on its way to the Arctic.
Q683923.w: Parallel grey, jagged ridges with small glaciers running north-west to south-east across north-eastern Yakutia, cut by a deep river gorge.
f: Its highest peak, Pobeda, meaning 'Victory', rises above 3,000 m.
Jan Czerski was exiled to Siberia after the Polish uprising of 1863.

q.q: Who is the Chersky Range named after?

Q2597340.t: Hilltop villages above valleys of morning cloud
Q2597340.s: In the Chin Hills, villages sit on the ridge tops rather than in the valleys, and on many mornings the valleys below fill with cloud. West of Myanmar's Irrawaddy plain, the land folds into ridge after ridge of steep, forested hills running north–south towards India. The highest summit, Mount Victoria, about 3,050 m, rises in the south.
Q2597340.w: Tightly packed north–south ridges of dark green forest, with clouds pooling in the valleys, west of the Irrawaddy plain.
f: Mount Victoria, also called Nat Ma Taung, is the highest point of the Chin Hills.
The hills continue north into the Indian states of Mizoram and Manipur.

q.q: What is the highest summit of the Chin Hills?

Q620493.t: Forest on one flank, steppe on the other
Q620493.s: The Tannu-Ola is a long east–west ridge where Siberia gives way to Central Asia. Its northern slopes, facing Tuva, are dark with larch and Siberian pine; its southern side, facing Mongolia, is bare steppe dropping towards the salty Uvs Lake. The contrast is striking: green on one flank, tawny brown on the other, with snow on the crest for much of the year.
Q620493.w: A long east–west ridge with dark forest on its northern side and bare brown steppe to the south, above a large salty lake.
f: Uvs Lake, south of the range, is the largest lake in Mongolia by area.
The Uvs Nuur basin is a UNESCO World Heritage site shared by Mongolia and Russia.

q.q: Which large salty lake lies south of the Tannu-Ola?

Q284226.t: The mountains a fabled old man tried to move
Q284226.s: A Chinese fable tells of Yugong, the 'foolish old man', who set out to dig away the Taihang Mountains because they blocked his door. His task looks hopeless: a long wall of ridges and sheer cliffs divides the high Loess Plateau of Shanxi from the flat North China Plain, running roughly north–south for some 400 km.
Q284226.w: A long escarpment of ridges and cliffs, with the flat, crowded North China Plain to the east and higher yellow loess country to the west.
f: In the fable, the gods were so moved by Yugong's persistence that they carried the mountains away.
Shanxi, the province west of the range, takes its name from it: 'west of the mountains'.
The Red Flag Canal, cut along its cliffs in the 1960s, brought water to farms in Henan.

q.q: What does Shanxi, the province west of the Taihang, mean?

Q1538623.t: Gullied loess ridges beside the Yellow River
Q1538623.s: In western Shanxi, the Lüliang Mountains run north–south between two rivers: the Yellow River on the west and its tributary the Fen on the east. Much of the range is draped in thick yellow loess, carved by erosion into a maze of gullies, terraces and flat-topped ridges. On the Yellow River just west of the range, the Hukou Falls pour muddy water into a narrow gorge.
Q1538623.w: Brown and yellow ridges furrowed by countless gullies, between the Yellow River's gorge to the west and the green Fen valley to the east.
f: The Hukou Waterfall is the largest waterfall on the Yellow River.
Loess on this plateau can be more than 100 m thick.

q.q: Which great river flows along the west side of the Lüliang Mountains?

Q1158071.t: Karst ridges, red cliffs and China's famous liquor
Q1158071.s: China's most famous liquor, Moutai, is distilled in a small town in these mountains. The Dalou Mountains rise between the Sichuan Basin and the Guizhou Plateau in steep, forested limestone ridges riddled with caves, sinkholes and gorges. The Chishui River cuts through them between glowing red sandstone cliffs, and on its bank lies the town of Maotai.
Q1158071.w: Parallel limestone ridges and deep gorges running south-west to north-east, between the red Sichuan Basin and the higher Guizhou Plateau.
f: The red sandstone landscape of Chishui is part of the 'China Danxia' UNESCO World Heritage site.
Moutai baijiu is distilled from sorghum in the town of Maotai on the Chishui River.

q.q: Which famous Chinese liquor comes from a town in the Dalou Mountains?

Q939398.t: A cliff edge between the Khorat Plateau and the plains
Q939398.s: The Dângrêk is less a range than a long step in the land. From the north, Thailand's Khorat Plateau rises gently to its crest; on the south side, cliffs drop sharply to the flat Cambodian plain, and the edge runs for some 300 km. Khmer builders used this dramatic brink: the temple of Preah Vihear, begun more than a thousand years ago, stands right on it.
Q939398.w: A long east–west escarpment with a gentle slope to the north and a steep, forested drop to flat plains in the south.
f: Preah Vihear temple became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2008.
In Khmer, Dângrêk means 'carrying pole'.

q.q: What does the Khmer name Dângrêk mean?

Q3109835.t: Forested ridges where South Asia meets Southeast Asia
Q3109835.s: Where India's north-east meets Myanmar, the land buckles into the Naga Hills, a tangle of steep ridges covered in forest and bamboo, with villages crowning the hilltops. Their highest summit, Saramati, about 3,830 m, carries snow in winter. In early summer the high Dzükou Valley near Kohima fills with lilies, and mist lies in the valleys most mornings.
Q3109835.w: Steep forested ridges running north-east to south-west along the India–Myanmar border, with villages dotting the crests.
f: Saramati, about 3,830 m, is the highest peak of the Naga Hills.
The Dzükou lily grows only in and around the Dzükou Valley.
Nagaland's Hornbill Festival, held every December, celebrates Naga cultures.

q.q: Which is the highest peak of the Naga Hills?

Q625425.t: A mountain range that carries on under the sea
Q625425.s: Running parallel to Myanmar's west coast, the Arakan Mountains form a long, forested wall between the Bay of Bengal and the Irrawaddy valley. Their western slopes take the full force of the monsoon, while the valley beyond lies in their rain shadow. The range does not really end at Cape Negrais: it continues under the sea and reappears as the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
Q625425.w: Long, parallel forested ridges running north–south close to Myanmar's west coast, with the broad Irrawaddy valley to the east.
f: In Burmese the range is called Rakhine Yoma.
Sittwe, on the coast west of the range, receives several metres of rain a year.

q.q: Which islands continue the Arakan Mountains beneath the sea?

Q1145416.t: Seven forested folds across central India
Q1145416.s: Satpura is often translated as 'seven folds', and the range does ripple across central India in long, forested ridges. It runs east–west between two of the few big Indian rivers that flow west to the Arabian Sea: the Narmada to the north and the Tapti to the south. In its sandstone heart lies the hill station of Pachmarhi, with gorges, waterfalls and ancient rock shelters.
Q1145416.w: Long, parallel forested ridges running east–west across central India, with the Narmada valley to the north and the Tapti to the south.
f: Dhupgarh, near Pachmarhi, is the range's highest point at about 1,350 m.
Satpura National Park is home to tigers, leopards and sloth bears.
Rock shelters around Pachmarhi hold paintings thousands of years old.

q.q: Which river flows along the northern side of the Satpura Range?

Q9177711.t: Snowy Tian Shan ridges above blue Sayram Lake
Q9177711.s: On one side of this snowy wall lies one of the greenest valleys in Central Asia; on the other, a dry desert basin. The Borohoro Mountains, in northern Xinjiang, separate the Ili valley, watered by moist westerly winds, from the Dzungarian basin stretching towards Mongolia. Near their western end sits Sayram Lake, a vivid blue alpine lake ringed by meadows.
Q9177711.w: A long snowy ridge running west to east, with the green Ili valley to the south and the pale Dzungarian plain to the north.
f: The Ili River flows west into Kazakhstan and ends in Lake Balkhash.
Sayram Lake lies at about 2,070 m.

q.q: Where does the Ili River, south of the Borohoro, end?

Q3182012.t: Among the wettest hills on Earth, with living bridges
Q3182012.s: When the monsoon blows north from the Bay of Bengal, the first high ground it meets is the Khasi Hills, and the clouds unload here. Mawsynram and Cherrapunji, on the southern edge, rank among the wettest places on Earth, with more than 11 m of rain a year. Khasi villagers train the roots of rubber trees across streams into living bridges that grow stronger with age.
Q3182012.w: Rolling green uplands ending in a steep edge above the flat, watery plains of Bangladesh to the south.
f: Cherrapunji holds the record for rain in a calendar year: about 26 m, in 1861.
Shillong, the capital of Meghalaya, lies on the plateau at about 1,500 m.
Meghalaya means 'abode of the clouds' in Sanskrit.

q.q: What does Meghalaya, home of the Khasi Hills, mean?

Q216593.t: Volcanic plateaus and a high blue lake
Q216593.s: South of the great Caucasus ridge, a second, lower mountain system runs across the southern Caucasus: the Lesser Caucasus. It is a jumble of folded ridges, forests and high volcanic plateaus dotted with old lava cones. Its centrepiece is Lake Sevan, a vast blue lake set at about 1,900 m, one of the largest high-altitude freshwater lakes in the world.
Q216593.w: Folded ridges and high, bare volcanic plateaus with the large blue Lake Sevan among them, south of the snowy main Caucasus.
f: Lake Sevan covers roughly 1,250 km².
The Sevanavank monastery stands on a former island in the lake, now a peninsula after its level fell.

q.q: At about what altitude does Lake Sevan lie?

Q519263.t: Hazelnut and tea slopes above the Black Sea
Q519263.s: Most of the world's hazelnuts grow along this coast, on the seaward slopes of the Pontic Mountains. The range rises steeply from Turkey's Black Sea shore and wrings the moisture out of the sea air, so its northern side is lush with forest, tea gardens and hazelnut groves, while beyond the crest the land turns dry and brown. In the east it climbs to about 3,940 m in the Kaçkar Mountains.
Q519263.w: A steep green mountain wall rising straight from the Black Sea coast, with drier brown uplands behind it.
f: Trabzon, on the coast below, was the capital of the Empire of Trebizond, a Byzantine successor state, from 1204 to 1461.
Almost all Turkish tea comes from the slopes around Rize.
The Sumela Monastery clings to a cliff face south of Trabzon.

q.q: Which crop covers the slopes around Rize?

Q170427.t: The 'old mountain' that named a whole peninsula
Q170427.s: Bulgarians call this range Stara Planina, the 'old mountain', and it is the one that gave the whole Balkan Peninsula its name. It runs some 550 km from the Serbian border to the Black Sea, a long green and grey wall across Bulgaria. At its southern foot lies the Rose Valley, where pink damask roses are picked each May and June for rose oil.
Q170427.w: A long east–west mountain wall across Bulgaria, with the Danube plain to the north and a narrow valley of fields along its southern foot.
f: Botev Peak, about 2,380 m, is the highest point of the range.
Bulgaria is one of the world's leading producers of rose oil.
The word Balkan is thought to come from a Turkic word for a wooded mountain range.

q.q: What does Stara Planina, the Bulgarian name of the range, mean?

Q208076.t: Bear country above Spain's green Atlantic coast
Q208076.s: Brown bears still roam the wild western end of these mountains. The Cantabrian Mountains run along Spain's northern coast and trap the moist ocean air, and the difference shows: north of the crest, green valleys, meadows and oak woods; south of it, the dry brown plains of the Meseta. Further east rise the jagged limestone Picos de Europa.
Q208076.w: A long east–west range close to Spain's north coast, green on the seaward side and brown on the inland side.
f: Somiedo Natural Park, in the western Cantabrians, is a stronghold of the brown bear.
Torre de Cerredo, about 2,650 m in the Picos de Europa, is the highest summit.
The Picos de Europa became Spain's first national park in 1918.

q.q: Which large animal survives in the western Cantabrian Mountains?

Q26955.t: Snow above Granada, within sight of Africa
Q26955.s: Snow on the southern edge of Europe, barely 40 km from the Mediterranean: the Sierra Nevada rises behind Granada to 3,479 m at Mulhacén, the highest point of mainland Spain. In winter its long white crest stands out against the brown hills of Andalusia, and on clear days the mountains of Morocco can be seen from the summit across the sea.
Q26955.w: A long, high, often snow-capped ridge just south-east of Granada, with the Mediterranean coast close by to the south.
f: Mulhacén is named after Muley Hacén, a 15th-century Nasrid ruler of Granada.
Its ski resort is the southernmost in Europe.
The Alpujarras, white villages on its southern slopes, were among the last Moorish strongholds in Spain.

q.q: What is the highest peak of mainland Spain?

Q686362.t: The dark hills where Spain's plateau meets Andalusia
Q686362.s: Heading south across Spain, the high Meseta ends at a long line of dark, wooded hills: the Sierra Morena. It runs some 400 km east–west above the Guadalquivir valley, never very high but rugged, covered in holm oak, cork oak and scrub. These quiet hills are a last stronghold of the Iberian lynx, and in their west lie the ancient copper mines of Río Tinto.
Q686362.w: A long line of dark, wooded hills running east–west, north of the broad green Guadalquivir valley.
f: The Despeñaperros pass has long been the main route from Madrid into Andalusia.
The Río Tinto, whose water runs red with dissolved metals, rises in its western hills.

q.q: Which endangered wild cat survives in the Sierra Morena?

Q3326866.t: An orange sea of sand in the Libyan Fezzan
Q3326866.s: Giraffes, elephants and crocodiles are carved into the rocks at the edge of this sand sea, drawn when the Sahara was green. Today the Idhan Murzuq in south-western Libya is a sea of orange sand hundreds of kilometres across, its dunes lined up in long rows and star-shaped peaks. The engravings are on the dark Messak plateau to the north-west, and the oasis town of Murzuq lies on the northern edge.
Q3326866.w: A vast field of orange dunes in south-western Libya, bordered by dark rocky plateaus to the north-west.
f: The rock engravings of Wadi Mathendous, in the Messak, are several thousand years old.
Idhan is a local term for a sand sea, like erg in Algeria.

q.q: What animals appear in the rock art near the Murzuq sand sea?

Q1537020.t: Star dunes and red oases in the western Sahara
Q1537020.s: The Grand Erg Occidental is one of the Sahara's great sand seas, covering some 80,000 km² of western Algeria. Its dunes pile up into huge star-shaped massifs and long ridges that glow orange at dawn. Around its edges lie palm oases such as Taghit and Timimoun, whose red mud-brick towns sit right against the sand, watered by underground channels dug centuries ago.
Q1537020.w: A huge sea of orange dunes in western Algeria, with dark palm oases along its southern and western edges.
f: Timimoun's gardens are watered by foggaras, underground channels bringing water from far away.
Some of its star dunes rise well over 100 m high.

q.q: What are Timimoun's underground water channels called locally?

Q1548386.t: The salt floor of a vanished giant lake
Q1548386.s: Racers have chased land speed records across this salt for more than a century. The Great Salt Lake Desert is the floor of Lake Bonneville, an ice-age lake that once covered much of Utah, and at its western edge lie the Bonneville Salt Flats, a crust so smooth and hard it works as a natural racetrack. Interstate 80 crosses it in a dead-straight line.
Q1548386.w: A vast white and tan salt flat west of the Great Salt Lake, crossed by a dead-straight highway towards the Nevada border.
f: Lake Bonneville was about 300 m deep at its peak, some 15,000 years ago.
Old shorelines of Lake Bonneville still show as terraces on the surrounding mountains.

q.q: Which ice-age lake left behind this salt desert?

Q272577.t: A desert named after a man who vanished in it
Q272577.s: In 1874 Alfred Gibson, a member of Ernest Giles's expedition, rode off across this country to get help and was never seen again; Giles named the desert after him. The Gibson Desert is a vast stretch of red sandplains, gravel and low dunes in the heart of Western Australia, dotted with spinifex and shimmering salt lakes. It remains one of the emptiest places on Earth.
Q272577.w: Endless red sandplains with gravel ridges, scattered dunes and pale salt lakes in the interior of Western Australia.
f: The Gibson Desert covers roughly 155,000 km².
Aboriginal peoples such as the Pintupi lived here long before Europeans arrived.

q.q: Who named the Gibson Desert?

Q767128.t: One of the hottest patches of ground on Earth
Q767128.s: Satellites have measured ground temperatures above 70 °C here, among the hottest surface readings on the planet. The Dasht-e Lut in south-eastern Iran is a desert of dark gravel, sand seas and, in the west, the kaluts: rows of giant wind-carved ridges like a fleet of stone ships, all pointing the same way. Together they look like a huge sheet of ribbed fabric.
Q767128.w: Rows of long, parallel wind-carved ridges, with dark gravel plains and sand to the east, in south-eastern Iran.
f: The Lut Desert became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2016.
In 2005 a satellite measured the land surface here at 70.7 °C.
The kaluts are yardangs, ridges sculpted by winds blowing steadily from the north.

q.q: What are the Lut's giant wind-carved ridges called locally?

Q1002.t: Asia's eastern tip, across the strait from America
Q1002.s: The Chukchi Peninsula is where Asia ends. Its tip, Cape Dezhnev, is the easternmost point of the Asian mainland, only about 82 km from Alaska across the Bering Strait. Most of the peninsula lies east of the 180th meridian, in the Western Hemisphere. It is a treeless land of bare hills, lagoons and tundra, where Chukchi and Yupik hunters have lived by the sea for millennia.
Q1002.w: A bare, hilly peninsula with lagoons along its coasts, reaching east to the narrow Bering Strait opposite Alaska.
f: Cape Dezhnev is named after Semyon Dezhnev, who sailed around it in 1648.
The two Diomede Islands in the strait lie on either side of the International Date Line.
On Yttygran Island, ancient hunters set up rows of whale bones known as Whale Bone Alley.

q.q: Who first sailed around Cape Dezhnev, in 1648?

Q3815319.t: Granite walls in 'the land that never melts'
Q3815319.s: Mount Thor's west face drops about 1,250 m, often called the greatest purely vertical drop on Earth, and it stands on the Cumberland Peninsula of eastern Baffin Island. This is a land of fjords, glaciers and sheer granite walls, much of it inside Auyuittuq National Park, whose Inuktitut name means 'the land that never melts'. The Arctic Circle runs right through the park.
Q3815319.w: A deeply fjorded, glacier-covered peninsula on eastern Baffin Island, with a large white ice cap and long fjords on either side.
f: The Penny Ice Cap covers about 6,000 km² of the peninsula.
Akshayuk Pass, a route of about 100 km through the mountains, crosses the Arctic Circle.
Pangnirtung, at the peninsula's southern gateway, is known for Inuit printmaking and weaving.

q.q: What does the Inuktitut name Auyuittuq mean?

Q837325.t: The northernmost point of the Eurasian mainland
Q837325.s: No mainland in Europe or Asia reaches farther north than this. Cape Chelyuskin, at the tip of the Taymyr Peninsula, lies at about 77°43′ N, less than 1,400 km from the North Pole. It is a low, bare shore of gravel and tundra facing the Vilkitsky Strait and the ice-capped islands of Severnaya Zemlya. Even in summer, sea ice often lingers along the coast.
Q837325.w: The bare northern tip of the Taymyr Peninsula, facing a narrow strait and the ice-capped islands of Severnaya Zemlya.
f: It is named after Semyon Chelyuskin, who reached it by sledge in 1742.
In 1878 the Swedish ship Vega, under Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld, became the first vessel to round the cape.
A polar station has operated here since 1932.

q.q: Who reached Cape Chelyuskin first, in 1742?

Q326917.t: China's rocky finger pointing into the Yellow Sea
Q326917.s: The Liaodong Peninsula points south-west into the Yellow Sea like a finger, almost closing off the Bohai Sea from open water. Its spine is a line of low, forested mountains, and its coast is rocky and indented with bays. At its tip lies Dalian, one of China's busiest ports; across the narrow Bohai Strait, the Shandong Peninsula reaches back towards it.
Q326917.w: A long, narrow peninsula pointing south-west between the Bohai Sea and Korea Bay, with a large port city at its tip.
f: The Bohai Strait between Liaodong and Shandong is roughly 100 km wide.
The Qian Mountains run down the middle of the peninsula like a backbone.

q.q: Which city lies at the tip of the Liaodong Peninsula?

Q1408929.t: The peninsula where Asia's last wild lions live
Q1408929.s: Asiatic lions survive in the wild in only one place on Earth, and it is on this peninsula. Kathiawar juts into the Arabian Sea between the Gulf of Kutch and the Gulf of Khambhat, a broad, mostly flat land of fields and scrub with a few isolated hills. The lions live in the Gir Forest in its south, not far from the revered temples of Somnath.
Q1408929.w: A broad, rounded peninsula in western India between two gulfs, flat and brown with a few rocky hills in the south.
f: More than 600 Asiatic lions now live in and around Gir.
Shatrunjaya hill at Palitana is crowned by hundreds of Jain temples.
Mount Girnar, about 1,070 m, is the highest point in Gujarat.

q.q: Which big cat lives in the wild only in and around Kathiawar's Gir Forest?

Q875712.t: Mainland China's southern tip, facing Hainan
Q875712.s: The Leizhou Peninsula is the southernmost tip of mainland China, a low tongue of red earth reaching towards the island of Hainan across the Qiongzhou Strait. It is surprisingly volcanic: old basalt flows cover much of it, and round crater lakes such as Huguangyan dot the land. Sugar cane, pineapple fields and eucalyptus plantations paint it in patches of green.
Q875712.w: A low, flat peninsula of red earth and green plantations, pointing south towards the large island of Hainan across a narrow strait.
f: The Qiongzhou Strait between Leizhou and Hainan is only about 20–40 km wide.
Huguangyan, a round crater lake, is part of a UNESCO Global Geopark.
Xuwen county, at the southern tip, grows a large share of China's pineapples.

q.q: Which large island lies across the strait from the Leizhou Peninsula?

Q913329.t: A stone table with cliffs above a vanished sea
Q913329.s: Sheer pale cliffs, called chinks, mark the edge of a huge stone table between the Caspian and the Aral Sea. The Ustyurt Plateau covers some 200,000 km² of bare clay, gravel and salt, and its chinks rise well over 100 m above the plains. On the eastern side they once looked out over the Aral Sea; now, as the sea shrinks, they overlook a desert of dried seabed.
Q913329.w: A vast flat plateau with bright white cliff edges, between the Caspian Sea and the dried-out bed of the Aral Sea.
f: Ancient hunters built long stone 'arrows' on the plateau to drive herds of saiga and gazelle into traps.
Saiga antelope, with their bulbous noses, still roam the plateau.

q.q: What are the cliffs at the edge of the Ustyurt Plateau called?

Q359194.t: Antarctic peaks first seen from Ross's ships
Q359194.s: In January 1841 James Clark Ross sailed into an unknown sea and saw great white peaks rising straight from the water. He named them the Admiralty Mountains after the officials who had sent him. They form the north-eastern tip of Victoria Land, with glaciers pouring between summits above 4,000 m. At their foot, on Cape Adare, the first people to winter on the Antarctic continent built huts in 1899.
Q359194.w: White peaks and glaciers rising straight from the sea at the north-eastern tip of Victoria Land, facing the Ross Sea.
f: Mount Minto, about 4,160 m, is the highest peak of the range.
Cape Adare hosts one of the largest Adélie penguin colonies in Antarctica.
The huts built at Cape Adare in 1899 are still standing.

q.q: Who named the Admiralty Mountains in 1841?

Q3861086.t: Dark peaks holding back the polar ice sheet
Q3861086.s: Along the western shore of the Ross Sea, the Transantarctic Mountains hold back the vast ice sheet of East Antarctica, and the Prince Albert Mountains are one stretch of that wall. Their dark rock peaks and nunataks poke through the ice for hundreds of kilometres, with great glaciers flowing between them towards the sea. Just to the south lie the famous ice-free Dry Valleys.
Q3861086.w: Dark rock summits poking through the ice along the western side of the Ross Sea, with glaciers flowing east between them.
f: James Clark Ross named them in 1841 after Prince Albert, husband of Queen Victoria.
They form part of the Transantarctic Mountains, which cross the entire continent.

q.q: Who were the Prince Albert Mountains named after?

Q1478409.t: Dinosaur bones high above an Antarctic glacier
Q1478409.s: Beside the Beardmore Glacier, one of the great rivers of ice through the Transantarctic Mountains, rises the Queen Alexandra Range. Shackleton's party climbed the glacier past these peaks in 1908 on their march towards the South Pole. High on Mount Kirkpatrick, the range's highest summit at about 4,500 m, geologists found bones of Cryolophosaurus, a crested dinosaur from a warmer Antarctica.
Q1478409.w: A long line of high, dark peaks beside a huge glacier flowing north from the polar plateau to the Ross Ice Shelf.
f: Shackleton named the range after Queen Alexandra, wife of King Edward VII.
Cryolophosaurus, about 190 million years old, was dug out of the mountain in 1990–91.
The Beardmore Glacier is about 200 km long.

q.q: Which dinosaur was found on Mount Kirkpatrick?

Q5460053.t: A chain of ice-buried volcanoes in West Antarctica
Q5460053.s: In Marie Byrd Land, far from any coast that visitors reach, a line of broad white domes rises out of the ice sheet. These are the volcanoes of the Flood Range, shield volcanoes so buried in ice that only their summits and craters show. The highest, Mount Berlin, reaches about 3,500 m and is considered potentially active. West Antarctica hides many more volcanoes beneath its ice.
Q5460053.w: A line of broad, smooth white domes rising above the flat ice sheet of Marie Byrd Land, far inland from the Amundsen Sea.
f: Mount Berlin, about 3,500 m, is the highest volcano of the range.
The range was first seen from the air during Richard Byrd's expeditions of the 1930s.

q.q: What are the peaks of the Flood Range?

Q4529916.t: Antarctic mountains named after a Detroit sponsor
Q4529916.s: In December 1929, Richard Byrd's expedition flew east over the Ross Ice Shelf and found a cluster of dark ranges rising from the ice of Marie Byrd Land. Byrd named them after Edsel Ford, son of Henry Ford, who had helped fund the expedition. Today the Ford Ranges show as scattered rock ridges and peaks, divided by broad glaciers flowing towards Sulzberger Bay.
Q4529916.w: Scattered dark ridges and peaks separated by wide glaciers, near the coast of Marie Byrd Land east of the Ross Ice Shelf.
f: Byrd's aircraft was a Ford Trimotor named Floyd Bennett.
Marie Byrd Land is named after Richard Byrd's wife.

q.q: Who were the Ford Ranges named after?

Q1253855.t: An ice-buried peninsula at the corner of the Ross Ice Shelf
Q1253855.s: At the eastern edge of the Ross Ice Shelf, a broad, ice-covered peninsula juts north into the sea. Robert Falcon Scott sighted it in January 1902 and named it after the new king, Edward VII. Almost all of it lies under ice, with only a few rocky ridges breaking through. In 1912 a Japanese expedition led by Nobu Shirase landed here, Japan's first exploration of Antarctica.
Q1253855.w: A broad, white, ice-covered peninsula at the eastern corner of the Ross Ice Shelf, with sea ice along its shores.
f: The Alexandra Mountains, among its few exposed rocks, are named after Queen Alexandra.
Nobu Shirase's ship, the Kainan Maru, reached its coast in 1912.

q.q: Which country's expedition landed on King Edward VII Land in 1912?

Q1641485.t: Mountains beside the largest glacier on Earth
Q1641485.s: Deep in East Antarctica, a chain of dark peaks lines the western side of the Lambert Glacier, often called the largest glacier on Earth. The Prince Charles Mountains poke through the ice for hundreds of kilometres, while the Lambert flows past them into the Amery Ice Shelf, draining a large share of the East Antarctic ice sheet. Australian surveyors mapped and named them in the 1950s.
Q1641485.w: Dark rock peaks and ridges poking through the ice beside a huge, slow river of ice flowing north into a floating ice shelf.
f: The Lambert Glacier is about 400 km long.
Mount Menzies, about 3,350 m, is the highest peak of the range.
They are named after Prince Charles, later King Charles III.

q.q: Which huge glacier flows past the Prince Charles Mountains?

Q6111566.t: Dark peaks scattered on the ice of Enderby Land
Q6111566.s: On the coast of Enderby Land in East Antarctica, a cluster of dark peaks and nunataks breaks through the ice sheet, about 40 km across. The Scott Mountains were sighted in 1930 by Douglas Mawson's expedition and named after Robert Falcon Scott. Around them the ice slopes gently down to Amundsen Bay and the Southern Ocean, a white world without a single permanent inhabitant.
Q6111566.w: Dark rocky peaks and nunataks poking through the ice just south of Amundsen Bay, on the coast of Enderby Land.
f: The surrounding part of Enderby Land holds some of the oldest rocks on Earth.
They were discovered by BANZARE, the British, Australian and New Zealand Antarctic Research Expedition of 1929–31.

q.q: Who were the Scott Mountains named after?

Q5306381.t: Some of the oldest rock on Earth, poking through ice
Q5306381.s: The Napier Mountains are a small group of dark peaks rising through the ice near the coast of Enderby Land. What makes them special lies inside: they give their name to the Napier Complex, rocks close to four billion years old that were once heated to more than 1,000 °C deep in the crust. From above they are just dark specks on an endless white sheet.
Q5306381.w: A small cluster of dark peaks on the white ice sheet near the coast of Enderby Land, east of Amundsen Bay.
f: Parts of the Napier Complex are among the oldest known rocks on Earth.
The mountains were discovered in 1930 by Douglas Mawson's BANZARE expedition.

q.q: What are the Napier Mountains known for among geologists?

Q1550766.t: A range found from the air and named for Shackleton
Q1550766.s: Rising from the ice east of the Filchner Ice Shelf, the Shackleton Range is a long block of dark mountains between two huge glaciers, the Slessor and the Recovery. It was spotted from the air in 1956–57 by the Commonwealth Trans-Antarctic Expedition and named after Sir Ernest Shackleton, who had dreamed of crossing the continent four decades earlier.
Q1550766.w: A dark, rugged block of mountains between two broad glaciers flowing west into the Filchner Ice Shelf.
f: The Commonwealth Trans-Antarctic Expedition completed the first land crossing of Antarctica in 1958.
Shackleton's own attempt to cross Antarctica set out in 1914 aboard the Endurance.

q.q: Which expedition first spotted the Shackleton Range, in 1956–57?

ne-rg-1730070769.t: The 'black mountain' of basalt in central Libya
ne-rg-1730070769.s: Its Arabic name, Jabal as-Sawdā', means 'the black mountain', and it could hardly fit better: a broad plateau of dark basalt lava lying across central Libya like a smear of soot. Roughly 100 km across, it rises from the pale desert around it with low, flat-topped cliffs. At its eastern edge lie the date-palm oases of the Jufra district.
ne-rg-1730070769.w: A broad, flat plateau of dark volcanic rock sharply outlined against the pale desert of central Libya.
f: Its dark surface is made of old basalt lava flows.
Sawdā' is Arabic for 'black'.

q.q: What does the Arabic name Jabal as-Sawdā' mean?

ne-rg-1730071505.t: Frankincense country above the Gulf of Aden
ne-rg-1730071505.s: Along the southern shore of the Gulf of Aden, a steep escarpment rises from a hot, narrow coastal plain to cooler highlands more than 2,000 m high. These are the Ogo Mountains, a band of limestone and granite in the Horn of Africa. On their dry slopes grow frankincense trees, whose fragrant resin has been traded from this coast since antiquity.
ne-rg-1730071505.w: A steep escarpment rising from a narrow coastal plain along the Gulf of Aden to a higher, drier plateau inland.
f: Frankincense is the dried resin of Boswellia trees, which grow on these slopes.
The hot coastal plain below is called the Guban, often translated as 'burnt land'.

q.q: Which aromatic resin comes from trees on the Ogo slopes?

Q5616476.t: Rain-soaked highlands where the Niger begins
Q5616476.s: The Niger is born here only about 250 km from the Atlantic, yet it sets off in the opposite direction, on a 4,000-km arc through West Africa. The Guinea Highlands of south-eastern Guinea are rolling, rain-soaked uplands, green with forest and savanna. At their southern edge, Mount Nimba lifts an iron-rich ridge above the forest to about 1,750 m.
Q5616476.w: Rolling green highlands with dark forest in the valleys, where the borders of Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire meet.
f: The Mount Nimba Strict Nature Reserve is a UNESCO World Heritage site shared by Guinea and Côte d'Ivoire.
The Nimba toad, found only here, gives birth to live young instead of laying eggs.

q.q: Which great river rises in the Guinea Highlands?

Q2895205.t: Eastern Ethiopia's highlands around walled Harar
Q2895205.s: East of the Rift Valley, Ethiopia's highlands continue as the Ahmar Mountains, a band of green ridges and terraced farmland above the dry lowlands. Their best-known town is Harar, an ancient walled city at about 1,900 m and for centuries a hub of trade and learning. The slopes around it produce Harar coffee, known for its fruity flavour.
Q2895205.w: Green ridges and terraced fields rising above dry brown lowlands in eastern Ethiopia, east of the Rift Valley.
f: Harar's walled old town, Jugol, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
In Harar, men traditionally feed wild hyenas by hand at night.
Ahmar means 'red' in Arabic.

q.q: Which walled city lies in the Ahmar Mountains?

Q1478180.t: Algeria's green coastal mountains above the sea
Q1478180.s: Along Algeria's Mediterranean coast, the Tell Atlas rises in a long chain of ridges and valleys, the greenest and most densely settled part of the country. Wheat fields, vineyards and olive groves fill the valleys, and villages cling to the ridge tops. In Kabylia, east of Algiers, the limestone crest of the Djurdjura climbs above 2,300 m and holds snow in winter.
Q1478180.w: A long band of green and brown ridges parallel to Algeria's Mediterranean coast, with fields in the valleys and the sea just to the north.
f: Lalla Khedidja, about 2,300 m in the Djurdjura, is the highest point of the Tell Atlas.
Tell comes from an Arabic word for 'hill'.
Atlas cedars grow on its higher slopes.

q.q: Which massif in Kabylia holds the Tell Atlas's highest peak?

Q633771.s: Behind Port Moresby, the land climbs into the Owen Stanley Range, the backbone of south-eastern New Guinea. Its ridges are steep, knife-edged and wrapped in cloud forest, rising to about 4,000 m at Mount Victoria. Named after Captain Owen Stanley, who charted this coast from HMS Rattlesnake around 1849, the range is so rugged that no road crosses it.
Q633771.w: Steep, cloud-covered ridges running along south-eastern New Guinea, rising just inland from Port Moresby.
f: Mount Victoria, about 4,040 m, is the highest peak of the range.
Its cloud forests are home to many species of birds of paradise.

q.q: Who was the Owen Stanley Range named after?

ne-rg-1730071583.t: New Guinea's snowy spine above hidden valleys
ne-rg-1730071583.s: Along the centre of western New Guinea run the Maoke Mountains, the highest mountains on any island, with ridges above 4,000 m and the last scraps of ice on Puncak Jaya. Dutch explorers called them the Snow Mountains. Tucked among them lies the broad Baliem Valley, home to the Dani people, which the outside world first saw only in 1938, from an American expedition's aircraft.
ne-rg-1730071583.w: A long chain of high grey limestone ridges and deep valleys along the centre of western New Guinea, often buried in cloud.
f: Puncak Jaya, about 4,880 m, is the highest summit of the range.
Richard Archbold's expedition spotted the populous Baliem Valley from the air in 1938.

q.q: What did Dutch explorers call the Maoke Mountains?

ne-rg-1730071603.t: Bare Arctic uplands on the divide of two oceans
ne-rg-1730071603.s: Across the far north-east of Siberia runs a broad upland of bare, rounded mountains, the Chukotka Highlands. They split the region's waters: rivers flowing north reach the Arctic seas, while those flowing south drain to the Bering Sea and the Pacific. There are no forests here, only tundra, stone and snow for most of the year, and the ridges look like crumpled grey paper.
ne-rg-1730071603.w: Bare, rounded grey mountains and tundra valleys across northern Chukotka, between the Arctic coast and the Anadyr basin.
f: The highest summits rise to only about 1,800 m.
Lake Elgygytgyn, in the uplands of central Chukotka, fills a meteorite crater about 3.6 million years old.

q.q: What covers the Chukotka Highlands instead of forest?

ne-rg-1730071613.t: Pacific shore, Arctic rivers: Siberia's narrow divide
ne-rg-1730071613.s: For hundreds of kilometres, the Dzhugdzhur range runs along the north-western shore of the Sea of Okhotsk, dropping steeply to the sea on one side and more gently to the Siberian taiga on the other. It forms a great divide: only a short distance from the Pacific coast, rain on its western slopes begins a long journey to the Arctic Ocean through the Aldan and the Lena.
ne-rg-1730071613.w: Bare, rocky ridges running parallel to the Okhotsk coast, with dark taiga valleys inland and a steep drop to the sea.
f: Its highest peak, Topko, reaches about 1,900 m.
The small port of Ayan lies at the foot of the range on the Okhotsk coast.

q.q: Which sea lies at the foot of the Dzhugdzhur range?

ne-rg-1730071631.t: One of the oldest mountain ranges on Earth
ne-rg-1730071631.s: The Aravallis are worn down to stumps, and no wonder: they are among the oldest fold mountains on Earth, their rocks raised well over a billion years ago. The range runs some 700 km across Rajasthan from Gujarat towards Delhi, a line of rocky, scrub-covered hills separating the Thar Desert in the west from greener plains in the east. Hill forts crown many of its ridges.
ne-rg-1730071631.w: A long, broken line of low rocky ridges running north-east across Rajasthan, with the sandy Thar Desert on the western side.
f: Guru Shikhar, at Mount Abu, is the highest point at about 1,720 m.
The walls of Kumbhalgarh Fort, in the Aravallis, run for more than 30 km.
Several Aravalli forts belong to the UNESCO site Hill Forts of Rajasthan.

q.q: Which desert lies west of the Aravalli Range?

ne-rg-1730071657.t: Western Afghan ridges with an ancient Greek name
ne-rg-1730071657.s: West of the Hindu Kush, Afghanistan's mountains fan out into long parallel ridges, known since ancient Greek times as the Paropamisus. They run east–west for hundreds of kilometres, bare and brown, with snow on the crests in winter. Between them flows the Hari Rud, whose valley leads west to Herat; hidden in one of its gorges stands the 12th-century Minaret of Jam.
ne-rg-1730071657.w: Long, parallel east–west ridges of bare brown rock in western Afghanistan, with the green thread of the Hari Rud valley between them.
f: The Minaret of Jam, about 65 m tall, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
The Hari Rud flows west past Herat and finally dies out in the Karakum Desert.

q.q: Which river flows between the Paropamisus ridges towards Herat?

Q1422726.t: Ocean floor lifted into Arabia's highest mountains
Q1422726.s: The rocks of the Al Hajar Mountains once lay at the bottom of an ocean. Here a huge slab of oceanic crust and mantle, the Semail ophiolite, was pushed up onto Arabia, and it is the best-exposed piece of sea floor on land anywhere. The range curves some 700 km through northern Oman and the UAE, dark and jagged, rising to about 3,000 m at Jebel Shams.
Q1422726.w: A dark, jagged arc of bare mountains parallel to the Gulf of Oman coast, from the Musandam tip towards Muscat and beyond.
f: Jebel Shams, about 3,000 m, is the highest point of Oman.
Oman's ancient falaj water channels, fed from these mountains, are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Wadi Ghul, beside Jebel Shams, is often called the Grand Canyon of Arabia.

q.q: What makes the Al Hajar Mountains famous among geologists?

ne-rg-1730071667.t: An 800-km cliff across the heart of Arabia
ne-rg-1730071667.s: West of Riyadh, the flat plateau of central Arabia ends at a sheer limestone cliff that runs for some 800 km, curving from north to south. The Tuwayq escarpment drops hundreds of metres to the desert below. At its most dramatic point, known as the Edge of the World, visitors stand on rock laid down in a Jurassic sea and look out across an endless plain.
ne-rg-1730071667.w: A long, pale cliff line curving north–south across central Arabia, facing west, with Riyadh on the plateau behind it.
f: The cliffs are built of limestone laid down in a shallow sea during the Jurassic.
Riyadh stands on the plateau just east of the escarpment.

q.q: Which capital stands on the plateau behind the Tuwayq escarpment?

Q217202.s: Across the middle of Romania, the Carpathians turn west and rise into their most alpine stretch: the Southern Carpathians, also called the Transylvanian Alps. Sharp ridges above 2,000 m separate Transylvania from Wallachia and stay snowy for half the year. In the Retezat Mountains dozens of glacial lakes glitter in rocky bowls, and at the range's western end the Danube cuts through the Iron Gates gorge.
Q217202.w: Sharp, often snowy ridges running east–west across central Romania, with the Danube gorge at their western end.
f: Moldoveanu, about 2,544 m, is Romania's highest peak.
Retezat, created in 1935, is Romania's oldest national park.
The Transfăgărășan road climbs over the range in hairpin bends to about 2,040 m.

q.q: Which river cuts through the Southern Carpathians at the Iron Gates?

ne-rg-1730071739.t: A lake-dotted upland above Alberta's boreal lowlands
ne-rg-1730071739.s: Despite the name, there is not a sharp peak in sight. The Birch Mountains are a broad upland of forest and lakes rising a few hundred metres above the boreal lowlands of northern Alberta, north-west of Fort McMurray, cut by streams and dotted with peat bogs. To the east the land drops to the Athabasca River valley and the oil sands.
ne-rg-1730071739.w: A broad forested upland with scattered lakes and bogs, north-west of Fort McMurray and west of the Athabasca River.
f: Much of the upland is protected as the Birch Mountains Wildland Provincial Park.
Woodland caribou and moose roam its forests and bogs.

q.q: Which river valley lies east of the Birch Mountains?

Q357546.t: A dome of ancient rock that is still rising
Q357546.s: The Adirondacks look like any old mountains: rounded, forested summits scattered with thousands of lakes. Geologically, though, they are unusual: a dome of very ancient rock that is still slowly rising, and not part of the Appalachian chain around it. Almost all of them lie inside Adirondack Park, which at about 24,000 km² is larger than Yellowstone, Yosemite, Glacier and Grand Canyon parks combined.
Q357546.w: A roughly round cluster of forested peaks and countless lakes in northern New York, between Lake Champlain and the St. Lawrence.
f: Mount Marcy, about 1,630 m, is the highest point in New York State.
Lake Placid, in the Adirondacks, hosted the Winter Olympics in 1932 and 1980.
Hikers who climb all 46 High Peaks are known as 'Forty-Sixers'.

q.q: Which Adirondack town has hosted the Winter Olympics twice?

Q1457996.t: Granite domes between the Guianas and Amazonia
Q1457996.s: Where Suriname, French Guiana and Brazil meet, the rainforest is broken by bare granite domes called inselbergs, rising like grey islands above the canopy. These are the Tumuc-Humac Mountains, a low, remote chain that forms the divide between rivers running north to the Atlantic coast of the Guianas and rivers flowing south into the Amazon basin.
Q1457996.w: Scattered bare grey granite domes above unbroken rainforest along the southern borders of Suriname and French Guiana.
f: Inselberg is German for 'island mountain'.
The French side lies within the Guiana Amazonian Park, one of the largest national parks in the European Union.

q.q: What are the bare granite domes above the forest called?

ne-rg-1730071811.t: Painted cliffs above the dry Brazilian backlands
ne-rg-1730071811.s: In the dry thorn scrub of Piauí, sandstone cliffs and canyons hide one of the richest collections of rock art in the Americas. The Serra da Capivara holds hundreds of painted shelters, where red figures of people, deer and capybaras hunt, dance and embrace across the rock. Some sites here have been argued to hold very early traces of people in South America, a debate that continues.
ne-rg-1730071811.w: Reddish sandstone cliffs and canyons rising from grey-green thorny scrub in south-eastern Piauí.
f: Serra da Capivara National Park became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1991.
Pedra Furada, a pierced rock, is the park's best-known landmark.

q.q: Which animal gives the Serra da Capivara its name?

Q7455221.t: A green escarpment above the dry sertão
Q7455221.s: On the border of Ceará and Piauí, the land rises abruptly in a long escarpment, the Serra da Ibiapaba, some 800 m high. Its top catches moisture from the Atlantic winds, so the plateau is green and cool while the sertão below is dry, thorny scrub. Near its edge, Ubajara National Park protects limestone caves reached by a cable car.
Q7455221.w: A long, steep north–south escarpment with a green plateau on top and dry brown scrubland below, in north-eastern Brazil.
f: Ubajara, created in 1959, is one of Brazil's smallest national parks.
The escarpment is gentle on the Piauí side and steep towards Ceará.

q.q: What does the Ubajara cable car take visitors to?

ne-rg-1730071825.t: Remote ridges named after a forest spirit
ne-rg-1730071825.s: On the border of Venezuela and Brazil, deep in the Amazon rainforest, low ridges and granite peaks rise from an unbroken green carpet. The Serra de Curupira takes its name from the Curupira, a spirit of Brazilian folklore who guards the forest, and whose backwards-turned feet leave tracks that lead hunters astray. Few places on Earth are farther from a road.
ne-rg-1730071825.w: Forest-covered ridges and a few bare rock peaks rising above an endless green canopy on the Venezuela–Brazil border.
f: In Brazilian folklore, the Curupira has red hair and feet that point backwards.
Rivers on its southern side flow towards the Rio Negro, the Amazon's largest left-bank tributary.

q.q: What is the Curupira in Brazilian folklore?

ne-rg-1730071835.t: The 'golden range' of Brazil's central highlands
ne-rg-1730071835.s: Serra Dourada means 'golden range', and in the dry season its quartzite ridges and grasslands do glow gold and ochre in the sun. The range runs across the highlands of Goiás, in the heart of Brazil's cerrado savanna, where rocky crests alternate with patches of twisted trees and, increasingly, the geometric fields of farms. Rivers here flow north into the Tocantins basin.
ne-rg-1730071835.w: Long, pale quartzite ridges and golden grassland amid cerrado and farmland in the highlands of Goiás.
f: Goiás was the scene of a gold rush in the 18th century.
The cerrado covers about a fifth of Brazil.

q.q: What does the Portuguese name Serra Dourada mean?

ne-rg-1730071839.t: Forested ridges on the Amazon's cattle frontier
ne-rg-1730071839.s: Dark forest on the ridges, pale pasture all around: the Serra dos Gradaús shows the Amazon frontier at a glance. This long line of forested hills rises in southern Pará, between the Xingu and Araguaia rivers. Rainforest still clothes the crests and the protected lands nearby, while much of the lowland has been cleared for cattle. The iron-rich hills of Carajás lie to the north.
ne-rg-1730071839.w: Dark forested ridges surrounded by pale rectangles of cleared pasture, between the Xingu and Araguaia rivers in southern Pará.
f: The Carajás mines to the north hold some of the world's largest iron ore deposits.
Pará is one of Brazil's biggest cattle-raising states.

q.q: Which two rivers frame the region of the Serra dos Gradaús?

ne-rg-1730071849.t: Table mountains and a thundering waterfall
ne-rg-1730071849.s: Where Guyana, Venezuela and Brazil meet, flat-topped sandstone mountains called tepuis rise from the forest with sheer walls hundreds of metres high. The Pakaraima Mountains include Mount Roraima, whose summit plateau, about 2,800 m high, is said to have inspired Arthur Conan Doyle's 'The Lost World'. On their Guyanese side, the Potaro River plunges 226 m in a single drop at Kaieteur Falls.
ne-rg-1730071849.w: Flat-topped mountains with vertical cliffs rising above rainforest and savanna where Guyana, Venezuela and Brazil meet.
f: Kaieteur is one of the most powerful single-drop waterfalls in the world.
The borders of Guyana, Venezuela and Brazil meet on the summit of Mount Roraima.

q.q: Which novel is Mount Roraima said to have inspired?

Q7446846.t: Borneo's north-western corner on the South China Sea
Q7446846.s: Here Borneo's coast turns a corner: the long western shore, facing the South China Sea, bends east towards Sarawak. The land is low and green, a mix of forest, swamp, rubber and oil-palm plantations, with forested hills rising behind long, straight beaches. The border between Indonesia and Malaysia runs close by, across the island's north-western tip.
Q7446846.w: Low green coast with long beaches, plantations and forested hills at Borneo's north-western tip, facing the South China Sea.
f: Borneo is the third-largest island in the world and is shared by three countries.
Tanjung Datu, the westernmost point of Sarawak, lies at this corner of the island.

q.q: How many countries share the island of Borneo?

ne-rg-1730071943.t: The 'land of thirst', a vast plateau of fossils
ne-rg-1730071943.s: The Great Karoo is a vast, dry plateau in the heart of South Africa, a land of flat-topped hills, dusty sheep farms and endless horizons. Its name is often traced to a Khoekhoe word meaning 'land of thirst'. Its rocks hold one of the world's great fossil records of mammal-like reptiles that lived more than 250 million years ago, distant relatives of mammals.
ne-rg-1730071943.w: Endless brown plains broken by flat-topped hills capped with dark rock, in the dry interior of South Africa.
f: The dark caps on its flat-topped hills are dolerite, a hard volcanic rock that resists erosion.
Karoo National Park lies beside the town of Beaufort West.
Karoo lamb is prized for a flavour said to come from the local shrubs the sheep graze.

q.q: What is the name Karoo often said to mean?

Q843903.t: Sandstone cliffs, desert oases and hidden crocodiles
Q843903.s: Crocodiles in the middle of the Sahara: in a few permanent pools of the Tagant, such as Matmata, they have survived since the desert was green. The plateau rises from the sands of central Mauritania in sandstone cliffs cut by deep gorges. Oasis towns such as Tidjikja shelter their date palms against the rock, and the old caravan town of Tichitt is one of the country's four ancient ksour listed by UNESCO.
Q843903.w: A broad sandstone plateau with dark cliff edges and sand-filled valleys, rising from the desert in central Mauritania.
f: Chinguetti, Ouadane, Tichitt and Oualata together form one UNESCO World Heritage site.
Stone-built Neolithic villages near Tichitt are more than 3,000 years old.

q.q: Which reptiles survive in the Tagant's desert pools?

Q3513709.t: A dead-flat stone plateau in the Algerian Sahara
Q3513709.s: Few places on Earth are as flat and empty as the Tademaït. This stony plateau in the middle of the Algerian Sahara stretches for hundreds of kilometres, a dark pavement of rock and gravel with almost no sand, plants or water. Its edges fall in low cliffs towards the oases around In Salah to the south and the Gourara oases to the west.
Q3513709.w: A vast, dark, dead-flat stony plateau in central Algeria, between orange sand seas to the north-west and north-east.
f: The oasis town of In Salah lies at the plateau's southern foot.
The Tademaït is a classic hamada, a desert of bare rock rather than sand.

q.q: Which oasis town lies at the southern foot of the Tademaït?

ne-rg-1730071987.t: Endless grass plains and giant cattle stations
ne-rg-1730071987.s: Single cattle stations here cover thousands of square kilometres. The Barkly Tableland, between the Northern Territory's red deserts and Queensland's Gulf Country, is a vast, almost treeless plain of black cracking soil and golden Mitchell grass. After the summer rains the grass turns green, and shallow lakes and swamps shine across the flat land.
ne-rg-1730071987.w: A vast, flat, nearly treeless plain of grass and dark soil, dotted with shallow lakes after rain, east of Tennant Creek.
f: Brunette Downs, on the tableland, covers more than 12,000 km², making it one of the largest cattle stations in the world.
Its dark clay soils crack deeply in the dry season.

q.q: Which grass covers the plains of the Barkly Tableland?

ne-rg-1730071991.s: Grey stripes along the streams betray nearly a century of gold mining in the Kolyma Uplands. North of Magadan, this land of bare, rounded summits, stony slopes and narrow valleys gathers the headwaters of the Kolyma, and its valleys have long been among Russia's richest sources of gold. The long Kolyma Highway winds through them towards Yakutsk.
ne-rg-1730071991.w: Bare, rounded summits and narrow valleys with grey mining scars along the streams, north of Magadan and the Sea of Okhotsk.
f: The Kolyma Highway runs about 2,000 km from Magadan to Yakutsk.
Gold was found in the upper Kolyma basin in the 1920s.

q.q: Which precious metal made the Kolyma Uplands famous?

ne-rg-1730071999.t: The steppe upland that splits Black Sea and Caspian waters
ne-rg-1730071999.s: It looks like no more than a gentle swell in the steppe, yet the Stavropol Upland splits the waters of the North Caucasus between two seas. Rivers on its western side join the Kuban and flow to the Sea of Azov, while those to the east, like the Kuma, head for the Caspian. Fields and ravines cover it from the Caucasus foothills to the Manych lowland, and Stavropol sits near its highest part.
ne-rg-1730071999.w: A broad, rolling upland of large fields and ravines north of the Caucasus foothills, with the city of Stavropol near its crest.
f: Its highest point, Mount Strizhament, reaches about 830 m.
Stavropol, founded as a fortress in 1777, stands at about 600 m.

q.q: Which sea do rivers from the upland's western side reach?

Q786792.t: Granite hills rising from the steppe above the Azov
Q786792.s: Strange piles of rounded granite boulders, the Kamiani Mohyly or 'Stone Tombs', break through the open steppe here. They are the tips of ancient granite hidden beneath the black soil of the Azov Upland, a low plateau of fields north of the shallow Sea of Azov, crossed by short rivers running south to the sea.
Q786792.w: Low, gently rolling steppe of large fields north of the Sea of Azov, cut by short river valleys running south to the coast.
f: Its highest point, Mohyla Belmak, is only about 324 m high.
The granite of the Azov Upland belongs to the ancient Ukrainian Shield.

q.q: What are the Kamiani Mohyly hills made of?

ne-rg-1730072065.t: Orange dunes marching down to the Senegal River
ne-rg-1730072065.s: Gum arabic, gathered from the acacias of these dunes, once made the emirs of Trarza rich. This corner of south-western Mauritania is a land of long orange sand ridges running towards the Atlantic, thorny trees and camel herds, stretching south to the green floodplain of the Senegal River. At the river the change is abrupt: sand right up to a ribbon of irrigated rice fields.
ne-rg-1730072065.w: Long parallel orange dunes running towards the Atlantic in south-western Mauritania, ending at the green ribbon of the Senegal River.
f: Rosso, on the Senegal River, is the region's main town and a ferry crossing to Senegal.
Diawling National Park protects wetlands of the Senegal delta on Trarza's southern edge.

q.q: Which river marks the southern edge of Trarza?

ne-rg-1730072069.t: Long sand ridges combed by the desert wind
ne-rg-1730072069.s: Inland from Mauritania's Atlantic coast, the Akchâr is a sea of long, straight sand ridges running north-east to south-west for tens of kilometres, pale gold with darker troughs between them. Few roads cross it and hardly anyone lives here. The dry north-easterly winds that shaped these dunes also push sand towards the coast and the capital, Nouakchott.
ne-rg-1730072069.w: Parallel pale-gold dune ridges running north-east to south-west, between Mauritania's Atlantic coast and the dark Adrar plateau.
f: The Akchâr is an erg, a desert of sand dunes rather than bare rock.
Its dunes line up with the prevailing north-easterly winds.

q.q: What is an erg, like the Akchâr?

Q3056158.t: Endless dune chains on the way to Mauritania
Q3056158.s: Not a single oasis interrupts the Erg Iguidi. This sea of sand in the far west of the Algerian Sahara stretches for hundreds of kilometres towards Mauritania: long, parallel chains of orange dunes, in places linked into rows of star-shaped peaks, with almost no tracks across them. It lies between the stony Hamada du Draa to the north and the ancient rocks of the Eglab to the south.
Q3056158.w: Long parallel chains of orange dunes running across the far west of Algeria, towards the Mauritanian border.
f: Its dune chains cross one of the least visited corners of the Sahara.
The town of Tindouf lies near its western end.

q.q: Which town lies near the western end of the Erg Iguidi?

Q3494060.t: Where the Rio Grande swings in a giant curve
Q3494060.s: In west Texas the Rio Grande, the border between the United States and Mexico, swings through a huge U-turn, and the land inside it is called Big Bend. This is Chihuahuan Desert country: pale, eroded badlands, cactus flats and, in the middle, the forested Chisos Mountains. The river slices through limestone in canyons such as Santa Elena, whose walls rise about 450 m.
Q3494060.w: A dramatic bend of the Rio Grande, cutting through desert and canyons, with a dark mountain island in the middle.
f: The Chisos are the only mountain range lying entirely within a US national park.
Big Bend has some of the darkest night skies in the lower 48 states.

q.q: Which river curves around Big Bend?

ne-rg-1730072577.t: An escarpment above a great African wildlife valley
ne-rg-1730072577.s: Across north-eastern Zambia, the high plateau ends abruptly at the Muchinga escarpment, dropping hundreds of metres into the broad Luangwa Valley. The contrast is plain: miombo woodland on the plateau, and below it the meandering Luangwa with its oxbow lakes. The escarpment is also a great divide, separating waters of the Congo basin from those of the Zambezi.
ne-rg-1730072577.w: A long, steep, wooded escarpment running north-east across Zambia, with the winding Luangwa River in the broad valley below.
f: The Luangwa Valley is famous for leopards and hippos, and for the walking safari, which began there.
Streams on the plateau side feed the Chambeshi, the most distant headstream of the Congo.

q.q: Which valley lies below the Muchinga escarpment?

Q559784.t: The last great stretch of Brazil's Atlantic Forest
Q559784.s: For some 1,500 km along south-eastern Brazil, a steep escarpment rises almost straight from the Atlantic: the Serra do Mar, the 'mountains of the sea'. Its slopes hold the largest surviving stretches of the Atlantic Forest, one of the richest and most threatened forests on Earth. On top lies the plateau where São Paulo and Curitiba grew; below it, beaches, bays and port cities.
Q559784.w: A steep, dark-green forested escarpment rising right behind the Atlantic coast of south-eastern Brazil, with a plateau on top.
f: Only a small fraction of the original Atlantic Forest survives, much of it on these slopes.
The railway from Santos to São Paulo, opened in 1867, climbed the escarpment on cable-hauled inclines.

q.q: What does the Portuguese name Serra do Mar mean?

Q1839756.t: The 'place of spirits' on Labrador's wild coast
Q1839756.s: At the northern tip of Labrador, bare, jagged mountains rise straight from the sea, cut by deep fjords and dotted with small glaciers. Their name comes from an Inuktitut word often translated as 'place of spirits'. The Torngat Mountains hold the highest peaks in mainland Canada east of the Rockies, and some of the oldest rocks on Earth, nearly four billion years old.
Q1839756.w: Jagged, dark, glacier-scarred mountains and deep fjords at the northern tip of Labrador, facing the Labrador Sea.
f: Mount Caubvick, about 1,650 m, is called Mont D'Iberville in Quebec; the border runs over its summit.
Torngat Mountains National Park was established in 2005.
Polar bears roam the coast in summer.

q.q: What is the Inuktitut name Torngat often said to mean?

Q1152132.t: The ridge where farmland gave way to the steppe
Q1152132.s: Where the Yellow River swings north in its great loop, a long mountain wall rises along its northern side: the Yin Mountains. To the south lie the irrigated fields of the Hetao plain and the cities of Hohhot and Baotou; to the north begin the grasslands and gravel of the Mongolian plateau. For many centuries this ridge marked a frontier between farmers and nomads.
Q1152132.w: A long east–west mountain wall rising abruptly from a flat green river plain, with the high, dry Mongolian plateau to the north.
f: Thousands of ancient rock carvings of animals and hunters have been found in the Yin Mountains.
Early sections of the Great Wall ran along these mountains more than 2,000 years ago.

q.q: Which great river loops south of the Yin Mountains?

Q1974954.t: Granite spires where the Yenisei breaks through
Q1974954.s: The Western Sayan runs north-east from the Altai towards the Eastern Sayan, a belt of taiga-covered ridges between the Minusinsk basin and Tuva. The Yenisei, one of the world's great rivers, cuts right through it in a deep gorge. In the Ergaki range, jagged granite peaks rise above alpine lakes, and one ridge, seen from the side, looks like a sleeping giant.
Q1974954.w: Long taiga-covered ridges with bare rocky crests, cut by the deep gorge of the Yenisei, between the Minusinsk basin and Tuva.
f: The 'Sleeping Sayan' in Ergaki is a ridge whose outline resembles a reclining man.
The Yenisei carries more water to the Arctic Ocean than any other river.

q.q: Which great river cuts through the Western Sayan?

ne-rg-1730072663.t: Deep taiga where a hermit family hid for decades
ne-rg-1730072663.s: The Abakan Range is a long ridge of dark taiga and bare summits running north from the Altai along the edge of Khakassia. Its forests are so deep and roadless that in 1978 geologists flying over the upper Abakan valley spotted a garden plot and found the Lykovs, an Old Believer family who had lived there cut off from the world for about forty years.
ne-rg-1730072663.w: A long north–south ridge of dark taiga with bare, rocky summits, west of the Minusinsk basin and north of the Altai.
f: Agafya Lykova, the youngest of the family, chose to stay on in the valley for decades.
The Abakan River rises here and flows north to join the Yenisei.

q.q: What did geologists find in the upper Abakan valley in 1978?

ne-rg-1730072703.t: Tea-covered hills and the highest peak of south India
ne-rg-1730072703.s: Once every 12 years, the neelakurinji shrub flowers and turns these hills blue. At the southern end of the Western Ghats, the highlands of Kerala and Tamil Nadu are carpeted with tea gardens, forest and grassland, and Anamudi, about 2,695 m, is the highest peak in India south of the Himalayas. The Ghats take the full force of the monsoon, and their forests are among the richest in species on Earth.
ne-rg-1730072703.w: Steep green hills with patchwork tea estates and misty grassy summits, inland from the Kerala coast in southern India.
f: The Western Ghats became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2012.
Munnar's first tea plantations were laid out in the late 19th century.
The Nilgiri tahr, a wild goat found only in these hills, lives on Anamudi's slopes.

q.q: What is the highest peak in India south of the Himalayas?

ne-rg-1730072715.t: The hills where pink 'Himalayan' salt comes from
ne-rg-1730072715.s: Rising abruptly from the plains of Punjab, the Salt Range is a line of rugged, reddish hills cut by gorges. It holds vast beds of rock salt, and the Khewra mine here, worked for centuries, is one of the largest salt mines in the world; most of the pink salt sold as 'Himalayan' comes from these hills. Their cliffs expose rock layers that geologists read like a history book.
